subtopic: REPATRIATION FROM THE FAR EAST- ARRANGEMENTS FOR RETURN OF CIVILIANS

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: REPATRIATION FROM THE FAR EAST- ARRANGEMENTS FOR RETURN OF CIVILIANS
speechtext:
The leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) asked me some days ago if I would give to the house a statement with respect to the repatriation of Canadian prisoners of war and civilians in the far east, letting the house have such information as would help to bring the position up to date. The statement I have to make is as follows:
All Canadian prisoners of war liberated at Hong Kong have, with one exception, been evacuated to Manila, where they are awaiting transportation to Canada. The exception is the case of one man whose lack of strength at the moment rendered it inadvisable for him to be removed.
Some 500 Canadian prisoners of war liberated in Japan have been evacuated, half to Manila and half to Guam. As of September 20, 1,086 prisoners of war have been officially reported safe in allied hands. Thirty-two liberated prisoners have already reached Canada and nineteen more are known to be on their way.
Brigadier Kay, Canadian Military Attache at Chungking, having completed his mission at Hong Kong, is now returning to Chungking.
Satisfactory reports on the progress of the liberation of Canadian civilians are being received. As was announced yesterday, a small group of eleven Canadian missionaries has already reached Oakland, California. Official word has been received of the liberation of 200 of the 600 known Canadian civilians. A list of these was recently given to the press. Some of the 600 are missionaries and persons who made their homes in the east and who may wish to stay there. On the other hand, there are a number of Canadians who are not known to us and a number of British subjects not included who will be coming to Canada to join their families here.
As reported in the press, Mr. E. H. Norman, of the Department of External Affairs, accompanied by two other officers of the department, has set up headquarters in Manila to look after arrangements for the relief and repatriation of Canadian civilians. They have been joined by two officers of the Canadian Red Cross whose primary function will be to look after the welfare of Canadian civilians.
It is hoped that the larger proportion of prisoners of war and civilians will be transported direct to Vancouver and arrangements have been made there by all the departments concerned, together with the Canadian Red Cross, for their reception. However, a certain number will arrive at United States west coast ports. The army has made arrangements for the reception of liberated prisoners of war and the Department of External Affairs has sent an officer to San Francisco who will be in touch with the United States authorities at all ports and with British consuls. The Canadian trade commissioner at Los Angeles will assist in the handling of any Canadians who may arrive there. In addition, the Canadian Red Cross will station one or two officers at San Francisco and will send on other personnel as may be needed from time to time.
Wheat and Barley

All prisoners of war and civilians arriving at United States west coast ports and destined for Canada will be sent to Vancouver. Provisions for medical care and for the supply of clothing, comforts and small luxuries are being made by the services for prisoners of war and by the Canadian Red Cross for civilians at all points where they are likely to arrive.
The Canadian government has informed the United Kingdom that the Canadian authorities and the Canadian Red Cross will be glad to afford every assistance possible for the repatriation of liberated United Kingdom prisoners of war and United Kingdom civilians from the far east who may be repatriated by way of Canada. If shipping facilities across the Pacific make it possible for the United Kingdom to make use of this route, large numbers of repatriates destined for the United Kingdom may arrive at Vancouver and be transported across Canada.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture) :
maintopic: MEASURES TO COUNTERACT REDUCED YIELD IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with the permission of the house and before you proceed with the next item I should like to read a statement on barley which I promised to the house yesterday.

Labour Conditions
Due to drought conditions extending over the greater part of the crop growing areas of western Canada the yield of barley has been greatly reduced and action has been taken to counteract this condition so that the live stock production programme of Canada will not be jeopardized.
In order to protect Canada's live stock feeding programme and because of the short crop of barley, the agricultural supplies board is of the opinion that all barley marketed in 1945^6 from the 1945 crop should be made available for the domestic market. With this in mind the feeds administrator advised the grain trade on August 22 last that no further export permits would be granted during the crop year 1945-46 for barley, whether whole, ground or processed.
To enable farmers to purchase and feed the higher grades of barley, some of which would normally receive a premium, when sold to domestic maltsters or exported, it has been decided as a temporary measure to add five cents to the advance equalization payment, thus raising the amount from fifteen cents to twenty cents per bushel on all barley marketed in the prairie provinces, the Peace River block of British Columbia and Creston-Wyndall area, British Columbia, during the crop year 1945-46. This increase will be made retroactive to August 1, 1945, on all barley delivered and sold since July 31, 1945, without receiving the malting premium. If any barley has been marketed and sold since that date without receiving the full five cents per bushel premium, then payment will be made up to the five cents. Regulations in this regard will shortly be released by the Canadian wheat board and these regulations will fix the effective date for payment at country points of the twenty cent advance equalization payments as farmers deliver their barley.
These regulations will also change the present methods of payment of malting premiums by domestic maltsters. Instead of paying the malting premiums to the seller of the barley, the maltsters will be required to pay five cents per bushel on all barley purchased into the equalization fund. The same system of paying the premium into the equalization fund will be used by exporters, if the assurance of domestic supplies will permit the export of some barley later in the crop year. The effect is, therefore, that the increase in the equalization payment replaces for the present crop year the malting premium that would otherwise have been paid to some farmers on barley sold to domestic maltsters or exported.
To further safeguard the feed situation throughout Canada, the present policy of
holding reserve stocks of feed grains at Fort William and in eastern Canada, on which the government pays interest and storage charges, has been extended to cover part of the prairie provinces and British Columbia.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in complimenting you upon your election to the high office of Speaker of this house let me also commend you for having drawn to the attention of hon. members the rule prohibiting the reading of speeches. If I am to judge by past years your task is not going to be an easy one; and as one of the twenty-five or so hon. members who have sat in the house since 1930 or prior to that year I await with some interest your enforcement of the rule, after the new members have made their maiden speeches.
We on this side may be pardoned if we seem to take pleasure at the return of the Liberal government to office in Canada after six years of war. It is a unique record in the political life of any government, and I think it well that we take note of the fact that in no other country has the government been returned after holding office during war-time. This government is faced with a difficult task in the period which lies ahead of us; but, as was pointed out by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the Minister of Reconstruction (Mr. Howe) our plans are being well and truly laid, and in fact are further ahead than those of any other country in the world to-day.
Much has been said about Canada's enviable record, and the splendid contribution in men and material this country has made toward the defeat of Germany and Japan. Another record has also been made, one which to my
mind will be of great help during the critical years lying ahead, and that is that this country for the first time has undertaken a great financial effort through and by its own people. We have not borrowed, nor have we had lend-lease; yet billions of dollars have been expended, all of which have been contributed by the Canadian people.
In an endeavour to be as brief as possible it is my intention to touch upon only one or two matters. In the speech from the throne the matter of a Canadian flag was touched upon, and has been discussed by some hon. members.
I think more people in Canada to-day will welcome the fact that the government has decided to have a Canadian flag. If the choice were left to me I could see none better than the one which flies above the parliament buildings. The red ensign is beautiful and distinctive, and carries all those symbols which I believe would please all groups in Canada. Certainly it is more striking than the flags of either New Zealand or Australia-and I shall refer to those countries later. If I were to change anything on the red ensign it would be to place thereon the maple leaf, something which I suggest might be done to good advantage. Now that we have decided to have a distinctive flag, I trust that any discussions in regard thereto will be free from recriminations from any section of the country.
Mention has been made of old age pensions. While I had not intended discussing that subject in this debate, I must say I was disappointed in the proposals for the betterment of the present old age pension plan, as outlined by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Claxton). I should like to see something more, and to have heard proposed a proper contributory system, retiring everyone who so desired at the age of sixty-five years. Under such a system, any person receiving the benefits would receive them by right rather than as a matter of charity.
I have one criticism to offer. When members of the C.C.F. party deal with social security measures, and proceed to tell what has been done in other lands, for reasons best known to themselves invariably they do not tell their audiences that in most of those countries, if not all, the people or the workers involved make a direct contribution toward the social security provided. By that omission they leave the impression that the money comes from the state as a whole; whereas, if one will look at the record concerning most countries, and particularly Great Britain, New Zealand and Australia, they will find that the people there, and especially the workers, pay in large measure-and, Mr. Speaker, as I shall show in a minute or two, they pay plenty.
The Address-Mr. Reid

The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) referred the other evening to conditions in New Zealand. Before proceeding to dissect his remarks may 1 point out that if we are to have discussions iL Canada about New Zealand or Australia, anc if it is to be suggested by any party that the policies in those countries are the ones we should follow, then I say for any sake let us have all the facts, not just part of them. I am prepared to discuss the facts, as I know them, from official records of New Zealand.

If the hon. member were to read my past speeches about New Zealand, she would find that I am perfectly well aware of the social measures of that country. What I have said is on the record.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre mentioned first of all, the price of food. If hon. members will recall, or will look at Hansard, they will find that I interjected, and that the hon. member was good enough to take his seat to permit me to ask a question. I asked him, if food was Cheaper in New Zealand, what were the farmers receiving?-because, after all, it is they who produce the food. Let me assure hon. members, however, that when one is dealing with percentages he finds that at times they do not always reveal the complete picture. Be that as it may, in the cost of living index for New Zealand it is shown that the cost of food is only some 29-52 per cent of the entire living costs. The remaining 70 per cent is made up of manufactured goods, including rents, all of which must be paid for. Those manufactured goods purchased by the people of New Zealand cost from two to four times as much as the same articles in Canada.
Not only are lower prices paid to New Zealand farmers, but their labour costs are higher, and the farm machinery they use- the same kind used in Canada-costs far more than the same machinery would cost in this country. Had I the time I would be prepared to talk costs in dollars and cents. Sometimes, I realize, that is not always a complete picture; but I could tell the house what farmers have to pay in butter, wheat and eggs for farm machinery in New Zealand, as compared with what like machinery would cost in Canada.

Is it any wonder that the leader of the opposition in New Zealand, whose, remarks must be taken to be just as authentic as those of the opposition to this government, who says that in New Zealand the farmer is the forgotten man? The Labour government of New Zealand are becoming perturbed about the farmer because they realize, that the stranglehold they have' on him and the things they have done to him are not going to last much longer. I ask hon. members to note what is now taking place in New Zealand. The New Zealand Labour government, which has few, if any, farmer cabinet ministers, are now out to take some representation away from the farmer constituencies. At the last election the farmers nearly outvoted them and so it appears that before the next election comes

Many people in this country are carefully watching the new government which was elected in Great Britain. I came, from that country in my early days, and it is my humble opinion that the people of Great Britain will ' take less during the serious days that lie ahead with better grace from a Labour government than they would do from a Conservative or even a Liberal government. Probably that is all to the good. Have you noticed however, the change in the attitude of certain people in this country and the United States since the Labour government was elected? We did not hear much about Great Britain from the C.C.F. members in this house before the war, although we heard a great deal against, the British empire and the British commonwealth of nations. Sir Keith was asked the reason for these failures, and this should be of interest to the people of Canada. I quote:
Why then have these socialist ventures failed in Australia? Sir Keith says that many of the Australian enterprises had capable managers 
who knew their business. The failure was due to other causes. Sir Keith puts them into a few paragraphs:
"Australians . . . are, alas, so very human that, when governments have gone into industry, those concerned have used their unions and their pressure politics, their votes and their influence to get personal advantages."
And again after observing that managers and executives were capable, he says, "They have been powerless against constant political interference, leading to over-development, overcapitalization and faulty finance."
And finally:
To-day nearly all these state enterprises are back in the hands of private enterprise after having proven inefficient and a huge drain on the taxpayers.
In fact to-day it is open to question whether Australia has more state enterprises than Canada, and they are not as successful as those in Canada. From what I know, Mr. Speaker, they are not nearly so successful as the government enterprises we have in Canada. I thought it advisable, in view of what the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre said in introducing this subject, that I should put the other side of the picture before the people of this country. In passing, if we are going to discuss these questions, I say let us have the
r"
entire picture. I do not want to be accused
as I was on former occasions, of intending by my remarks anything derogatory to the people or the country of New Zealand, but I do feel that when a party in this house is constantly dangling before the people of Canada what New Zealand has been able to
accomplish, we ought to know just what the facts are. These hon. gentlemen have been pointing to New Zealand with pride for three or four years, but before the people of this country turn over all they have to an untried socialist government, I say we should know what the actual facts are about New Zealand and Australia.

It was not my intention, Mr. Speaker, to say one word about the Japanese this afternoon, but the subject has been introduced into this debate. I have one question to propound to the member for Winnipeg North Centre, who spoke of the great deeds of the men of the Winnipeg regiment, who are now returning from Hong Kong. When it comes to the time to dispose of the Japanese in Canada, I am just wondering whether my hon. friend would leave the decision in that matter to those Winnipeg men who are returning from Hong Kong. If he would not, I would like him to tell the house why these men should not have some say in this matter. I do not want these words of mine, Mr. Speaker, to be twisted around outside this house, as they have been before, to make it appear that I nurse some racial hatred against the Japanese. Those are tactics that have been resorted to in the past; they could not discount the arguments that we put up, so they talked of racial hatred.
May I say to those who have become the champions of the Japanese in this country, that I would be willing to abide by the vote of the people of British Columbia; and if that is not the democratic way to settle it, I would like to hear why it is not. I would like to be told a better way. I am sure that if this question were left to a vote of the people of British Columbia there would be no doubt as to what would be done with the Japanese in this country.

In closing I want to say one word about the atomic bomb. I think Canada has been rather too timid and backward in not seeking to take some credit for the development of the atomic bomb. Canada supplied the minerals, the scientists and other kinds of help in its development, and we are just as much entitled to credit, if credit is due, as is the United States. If I had my way, though, I would not divulge the secret of the atomic bomb to any other country, because if we pass the information around it is going to be more difficult indeed to keep it a secret. God forbid that there should be another war! But who can tell? When one looks round at the multitudes of people in the various countries some of whom are beginning to arm, I think that from a practical point of view we should keep that secret to ourselves, because the day may come when we may have to use it again.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in opening my remarks to-day may I, as so many others have done, congratulate you on your appointment to the high office which you now hold, and may I say that judging from the manneT in which you have fulfilled the duties of your office since the opening of the house, I am1 convinced you will preside over our deliberations not only with fairness but with quiet dignity and kindliness; that means so much to every member in the chamber. I believe you are a worthy successor to our former Speaker, the present minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Glen), who also possessed these gracious attributes in a very large measure.
The attitude of the government in this debate has taken quite a change during the last few days. When the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) rose to reply to the speech of my leader, the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken), he acted) as though there were nothing to answer-nothing had been Brought out that was even worth answering. He went

The Address-Mr. Green

on to boast a bit about the election results, and I could not help admiring his nerve in doing so. Here we have a government which had approximately half its supporters defeated in, a general election, now holding office by the support of a group of members who were formerly independent, a group who have shown considerable facility in changing their political coat, a group who will not be very comforting people to have behind one in a pinch, and yet the Prime Minister says: "Oh, well; we won a great election; what is there to complain about? Let us get on with the business of the house."
A few days after that, on Friday last to be exact, the Prime Minister went to his new riding of Glengarry. Apparently he is going to keep up his political fences a little better this time than, he did in the last parliament. He went to the annual fair, and according to the press he made certain statements. He is reported as follows.
Mr. King said that the three most important things facing Canada to-day were demobilization, employment and housing.
So that so far as he at least is concerned the amendment offered by the official opposition has had some effect.
Now I notice that the ministers are being smoked out of their holes; they are coming out and making statements, and the whole attitude of the government is not at all as smug as it was a few days ago. I suggest they would be very well advised not to try to assume that smug attitude at any time from now on until the end of this parliament, because they are very much under thie observation not only of members on this side of the house but also of the Canadian people.
I have mentioned' the main facts set out in our amendment. Let me read the amendment again for the benefit of all our friends to the left. I do not see* how any one of them who is dissatisfied with the government's progress on the questions mentioned in the amendment can conscientiously vote against it. I quote:
We respectfully submit to Your Excellency that Your Excellency's advisers have:
(a)	failed to demobilize our armed forces on a fair basis and, in particular, have failed to prevent serious disadvantage to overseas service personnel:
(b)	failed to provide a speedy and effective plan of reconversion from war to peace, and failed in particular to join in partnership with labour and industry in devising a workable scheme to provide jobs, with fair wages, for discharged service personnel and war workers;
(c)	failed to take adequate and timely action to meet the ever-mounting housing crisis.
To-day I propose to say a few words about demobilization and housing, to emphasize two

features of reconversion which have not yet been dealt with to any extent in this debate, and to conclude with some remarks on Canada's policy or lack of policy in the Pacific.
First of all, demobilization. Our amend*-ment sets out the position of members of the Progressive Conservative party, and it has been adequately dealt with by various speakers from our party. But yesterday there appeared in the press certain statements from overseas which I think require an explanation from the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Abbott). They deal with the repatriation of N.R.M.A. troops overseas. They allege that N.R.M.A. men who were forced to go abroad, and who were never in action, are being sent home ahead of men who fought. Apparently this is being done because these N.R.M.A. men have a high point score, most of such points earned by long service here at home in Canada.
This article quotes from the Amsterdam edition of Maple Leaf, which is a Canadian army newspaper and as such is entitled to the most careful consideration of every member of the house. The clipping says:
The editorial asked why National Resources Mobilization Act personnel who hadn't left the United Kingdom for Europe by V-E day now were returning home with the first division

Not the fourth or the fifth division, if you please, but the first. It added that thirty-one per cent of a draft from the Saskatoon Light Infantry, support battalion of the first division, consisted of N.R.M.A. personnel. It went on to put the situation clearly:
This sort of business isn't funny. Men who volunteered to come overseas, who either went into action as volunteers or did their best as volunteers, to see that the fighting men were equipped with the necessaries deserve better treatment. This is an appeal on behalf of the volunteers who made the Canadian army an army of which to be proud. All that is wanted is justice.
That statement by the army paper seems very fair, and I think the government policy, if it is as alleged in the army paper, is very unfair. The Canadian people do not believe in a policy of that type. I suggest to the Prime Minister and his Minister of National Defence that the Canadian people from one coast to the other believe that N.R.M.A. troops who are available should be used for the army of occupation and that those still in Canada should be sent over to relieve the volunteers as soon as shipping can be arranged.
Then, housing. Like demobilization, it has been dealt with by those who have preceded me in this debate. I think it is largely a question of supplies. After all, we have every-

The Address-Mr. Green
thing here in Canada to build houses. The problem is to turn our resources into buildings. I advocate that the government should lead an all-out drive, the same sort of drive that enabled us to build ships and tanks. There is not yet any evidence that an all-out effort to solve this housing problem has been made. The government have many war plants; surely some of them could be put to use for the production of supplies and equipment needed for buildings. I see by this week's press that in the United States all restrictions on construction hawe been removed. Perhaps the time has arrived when that should be done in Canada too. The construction industry in Canada has always been a progressive and up-to-date industry. I know that is true in the west. Men engaged in building have always been a good deal ahead of most othei industries, and I am sure that if they are given their heads, if they are given every encouragement, they can provide the buildings much more rapidly than buildings have been provided in the last few months. I agree that houses are the first need, but the need does not stop there. There is a great need for small stores. Hundreds of houses have been put up with no stores to service them. Office space is needed. Doctors being demobilized from the forces are unable to get offices. The same thing is true of other professional and business men. This question of building is going to be of vital importance to Canada for a long time to come.
So far as office space is concerned I suggest to the Prime Minister that he have a survey made of all the office space in Canada being used by governmental departments. I know in my city of Vancouver there are government departments scattered around in practically all the large office buildings; they are in the very best space available in the city. At the same time we have the government using the old Vancouver hotel as an army headquarters. I am quite sure that many of the governmental departments could be put into that hotel, thereby freeing large areas of office space. Probably the same condition exists in many other centres in Canada.
I now come to reconversion. The first feature of the reconversion plan is the complete and utter failure to consider the human factor. Let me take you to Vancouver. On V-J Day, August 14-and no doubt the situation was exactly the same in other cities in Canada-the people were rejoicing; everybody was happy because at last this terrible war had ended. Within forty-eight hours- in fact within twenty-four hours in many cases-thousands of our citizens were thrown 47696-21J
out of work, not knowing where to turn. I think the minister responsible for that policy failed to realize its effect on the people. And, mind you, the Minister of Reconstruction said something the other night which shows that he deserves a lot of blame for that policy. At page 227 of Hansard he used these words:
Personally I am the last man entitled to claim surprise at the end of the war, having known months in advance the approximate date of the use of the atomic bomb.
There might have been some excuse for him and his department if he had no idea when the war would end, but certainly the man on the street, the man in the war job, had no way of knowing that the war was about to end. He was being told by the press and public men that it would go on into 1946. There was not the slightest suggestion that it was about over. He had been making a great contribution; had considered himself a partner with his loved ones overseas. Remember that many of our fighting men came from families the heads of which were engaged in this war work. These people in war work were high-spirited; they had answered every appeal made by the government; they were paying heavy taxes with not much chance to save; many of them were putting what little they could save into houses and trying to become established; and then immediately after V-J Day they were thrown out of work. They were told to get out to the woods and the mines. Many of them were not physically fit to do so. Many of them, by this time skilled tradesmen, were told, "You go out and get a job in the woods." Very little sympathy was shown to them in official quarters. They were treated as though they were a commodity like lumber or steel; and, Mr. Speaker, that shook the confidence of the people in the whole reconversion plan of the government. It affected not only war workers but also men and women engaged in ordinary peace-time activities. Everybody was jittery. They said, ''Am I going to lose my job too?" It had a bad effect on the morale of the people in our province; also it was a bad example to set for private employers; it gave the private employer an excuse to fire people in just the same way. I think it is a very serious matter that the official mind worked in this way, and if it worked in that way on V-J day it will do so again. To me that is a very serious matter. It might have been all right in 1939-I do not think it was, even at that time-but since then there has been a steadily increasing value placed on people, placed on the human factor. The whole trend has been in that direction. Take the
The Address-Mr. Green

trend of legislation passed in this house-the social security legislation,; the whole trend has been to think of people before we think of material things and of wealth. The Atlantic charter promised freedom from fear and freedom from want. That is what the Canadian people expect. Instead, after V-J day they got this vindictive treatment; were thrown out of work without any warning. I suggest to the Prime Minister that is not good enough in 1945 from any government, federal, provincial or municipal.
It was not necessary. Other methods could have been used. The Minister of Reconstruction and other members of the government could have explained to the Canadian people that there was now a great need for men in the construction industry, in the woods and in the mines. They couldi have asked them to change over, to take these jobs in other industries. They could -have called on the shipyards in Vancouver-and I use Vancouver only as an example-to release a certain number of construction workers, of miners, of loggers, and might have augmented their wages for a period of three or four months until th-ese Canadians had become reestablished in other industries.
I also think some provision might have been made for the expense of moving, and there could have been a delay in the dismissals, rather than throwing people out by the thousands without any notice, as was done.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: The hon. member says, "without any notice". They were given seven days' notice.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I was there; I know what happened. They were given seven days' pay and kicked out. That is what they were given. The picture is this: it was put clearly by the hon. member for Vaneouver-Burrard (Mr. Merritt) in a speech I heard him make during the election campaign, and no one had a better right than he to make the statement. He said: "You can lead a Canadian anywhere, but you cannot drive him one inch." That should have been in the minds of the government in starting their reconversion plan.
Let me refer now to the second feature of the reconversion programme. The Minister of Reconstruction the other night used the words, "peace-time pattern of employment." What does that mean? It means that we either have or will have a pattern of employment for peace-time, a plan that will say which industries are to be maintained and which industries are to be allowed to die, that will say, as a result, where people are to get jobs. That decision is in the hands of, the dominion government to a greater extent than ever

before. They have these government plants; they have interests in other plants operated by private industry; they are placing many orders; they have great influence in marketing, in deciding where our goods are to be sold and what goods are to be sold; in producing and distributing materials; and through the industrial development bank. * It is largely in the hands of the dominion government to-day to determine what industries are to be maintained in Canada and where the people will have to go to work. That pattern, if there is one, should be made public, for every portion of the country is vitally interested. Take as an example the people of British Columbia. We should know the pattern, should have a chance to discuss it with the government, and to take some steps at least to help maintain industries which we believe should be carried on into peacetime. Now we are working in the dark; there is too much uncertainty.
Let us look for a moment at the aircraft and shipbuilding industries in British Columbia. At one time the Boeing aircraft plant employed, either directly or through its subsidiaries, over ten thousand people. Men and women were working not only in Vancouver but in other centres throughout the province, doing a great job. In the United States the bulk of aircraft manufacturing is done on the Pacific slope; yet now in Canada that Boeing plant has been shut down. We would like to know whether it is the policy of this government to stop manufacturing aeroplanes on the Pacific coast and, if so, why that has been done.
At one time -we had more than thirty-three thousand men engaged in shipbuilding in British Columbia, and in that province we turned out over seventy per cent of all the merchants ships produced by Canada. Many other subsidiary engineering industries were built up, and in fact industries of all kinds; many skilled workers were trained. Now there have been extensive lay-offs. There is some talk that in future our shipbuilding industry will have to go on a repair and maintenance basis, merely doing the repairing of ships. That happened after the last war. We had a flourishing shipbuilding industry on the Pacific coast then, but after the war it died. It is true that at present some government work is continuing, but there is no certainty about the future. This government has not announced any policy in regard to shipbuilding, and really there is no excuse for not having done so. In July of last year the Canadian shipbuilding and ship repairing association presented to the government a brief in connection with shipbuilding; various representations

The Address-Mr. Green
have been made by labour unions and by members of the last parliament; yet no one knows just what the shipbuilding policy is to be. Last September it was announced that an interdepartmental committee was being set up to review the proposals submitted by the shipbuilders. I do not know whether that interdepartmental committee has ever met. It was supposed to meet and then the shipbuilders were to be called in. Labour union leaders also should have been called in, but no promise ever was made that this would be done. Apparently there have been no results, although all this happened over a year ago. Now what do we see happening? The Canadian Pacific Railway Company, one of the firms which will be requiring many ships, is placing its orders in Great Britain. I have a press dispatch, dated August 28, to the effect that their first freighter already has been launched at Glasgow, and that three more are to be produced in Great Britain. The Canadian Pacific Railway Company will require many passenger ships, both for transoceanic service and for coastal service. The same is true of the Canadian National Railways. Is it the policy of this government that Canadian companies are to be required to use Canadian ships? We must have a peace-time pattern for both the aircraft and shipbuilding industries, and we must have it at an early date.
So much for the amendment of the official opposition. In conclusion I come to the question of Canada in the Pacific. The centre of world activities either is shifting or has already shifted from the Atlantic to the Pacific. Far-reaching decisions are being made in that area this very day. As an example take the decision as to what treatment is to be meted out to Japan. It seems clear that a very strong hand will be required. That is something which should be of concern to every Canadian. Press dispatches show so clearly the attitude being taken by the leaders of that country. I have here a press dispatch dated August 15, which tells of a Tokyo broadcast by the chief of the Japanese broadcasting corporation's overseas bureau, one Kusuo Oya, who was broadcasting to the troops on the fighting fronts telling them about the surrender. The Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) laughs; I have no doubt he has had to learn a great many Japanese names since he took over the administration of the Japanese in Canada.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: When you pronounced that name I said you were doing pretty well.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
This broadcast is significant, because here is what the man said:
We have come to a point where it is useless to resist the enemy further. We have bowed to the enemy's material and scientific power.
. . . We have lost, but this is temporary.
The press dispatch goes on to say:
Oya added that Japan's mistake was the lack of "material strength, necessary scientific knowledge and equipment," and declared: "This mistake we must amend."
A few days later we had a dispatch in which the sultan of Johore quoted the former Japanese commander of Singapore as saying:
We hope that peace will last for twenty years, and then we will be back here again.
Then General Wainwright, that heroic soldier who led the United States troops in their last stand on Corregidor, told the American people the other day that no soft peace must be given to the Japanese, and according to the press dispatch he stated that the Japanese-
. . . are not sorry for what they have done to countless thousands. . . .
They are not sorry for the torture they have inflicted. ... It simply would not occur to them to be sorry, because they have done nothing which is at variance with their accepted philosophy.
That is the point which should be clearly understood. I am a soldier and I do not pretend to know how long will be required or by what steps the bestial elements in their nature can be eradicated.
But until we are assured that these qualities have been extinguished-not simply submerged -then the Japanese nation, powerless as it is to-day to make war, will remain a menace to our world.
A strong hand is needed with Japan, and Canada's voice should be heard. The Canadian flag should be flying in Japan to-day. Other nations are showing great interest in the Pacific. Here we have the United States planning now for bases in different parts of that ocean. Russia is edging in, having moved into Manchuria. I have a dispatch dated September 4, which reads:
The Soviet Khabarovsk radio said to-day that Russia is planning a large scale development of her northeast Pacific coast and will build new harbours on the Kamchatka peninsula opposite Alaska.
Khabarovsk also told men of the Red army that Russia would turn the twenty-odd islands of the former Japanese Kurile chain into "varitable bastions forming a screen of steel" protecting Russian Pacific wTaters.
Australia also is talcing a great interest and demanding that she be treated as a principal power in the Pacific, not as a subsidiary power. There is also the question of trade. Everyone knows how vital it will be to Canada to develop a great trade across the Pacific ocean.
Canada should be one of the principal powers in the Pacific. And yet, what is

The Address-Mr. Green
Canada's Pacific policy? Nowhere is our position more uncertain. Throughout, the government have been hesitant. True, Canada was the first to declare war on Japan. Then we had the ill-fated expedition to Hong Kong. When it came to taking part in the Pacific council the Prime Minister had to be pressed before he would have this nation join the council. He took the position that it only had to do with the southwestern part of the Pacific; that there was no hurry for Canada to join it.
Then came the Kiska force in August, 1943, when Canada sent troops up to that island. But when the island had been taken, Canadian troops were not sent on to take part in the fighting on the other islands of the Pacific, as had been done with the United States troops. Oh, no; they were brought home, and they did no fighting whatever until more than a year later, when some of them were forced to go over to Europe.
Within the last few weeks we have had the spectacle of the Canadian cruiser Uganda taken from the firing line across the Pacific and brought back to Canada, because of the man-power policy of this government for the Pacific-something which did little good to the fair name of Canada around the Pacific shores.
At the present time the government shows little sign of being interested in the Pacific. Well, the Canadian government, the Canadian parliament and people would be well advised to watch very closely what goes on around the shores both of the Pacific and of the Arctic, as well as the Atlantic. Canada must be prepared to play her full part, and the government must take the lead.
Finally I would say a few words about this House of Commons. We are most fortunate in having among our number so many new members who have served in the armed forces of the country during this last war. Those who have spoken have shown clearly- oh, so clearly-that they have an important contribution to make to Canada's public life. They and their comrades are the greatest asset of this nation. The young men and women who have been in the fighting forces of Canada are the biggest asset of this nation to-day, and will be in the years to come.
Hon. members of those forces who have taken seats in this chamber have shown a fine spirit. I might add, too, that that same fine spirit has been shown by other new members who were not privileged to serve in the forces. There is on the part of members of the house a keenness to serve which I suggest is truly remarkable; to me it ha( been

inspiring. In the years which lie ahead I am sure the house can, if it so chooses, give the Canadian people real leadership.
Many Canadians have been afraid of the post-war years. There have been many head-shakers, many prophets of doom. They have been wrong. Canada has come through the war stronger than ever, largely because of the character, courage and intelligence of the individual Canadian. Canadians can surmount every obstacle in the future; but let me repeat that this House of Commons has a duty to give them bold and straight-forward leadership in facing such obstacles.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in the debate I should like first to associate myself with the concluding remarks of the hon. member who has just spoken (Mr. Green). At first I had not intended speaking in the debate. I had been enjoying the valuable contributions made by the younger members who appear for the first time in the house. The contribution not only of members from the armed forces but that of other members has been of a high standard indeed, and one of which we may well be proud.
A further reason for refraining from taking part in the debate was that during the six sessions I have been here it has always seemed to me we have spent too much time on the debate in reply to the speech from the throne. In those sessions we spent on this debate periods ranging from two to six weeks, with the result that invariably in the last few days of each session we found ourselves passing millions of dollars' worth of estimates without having given them proper consideration. Therefore in future sessions I suggest we give some consideration to having this debate conclude when the various leaders of the groups in the house have spoken. I would ask that this suggestion be taken into consideration.
To-day I was moved to take part in the debate because of what was said yesterday by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) respecting the setting of a floor price under wheat for the next five years. This is a matter of great importance not only to western Canada but to agriculture throughout the dominion. Let me say at once that I am not objecting to order in council P.C. 6122, which sets a ceiling price of $1.55 on wheat for export. It seems to me the reasons given by the minister for the setting of that ceiling price are logical and carry great weight. Under the conditions existing in Europe there is every reason why we should contribute to their betterment. I would point out however that in doing so we should not place the burden upon only one section of our Cana-

The Address-Mr. Wright
dian economy. Under this order in council that is what we may be doing, especially if we allow the floor price of $1 a bushel, f.o.b. Fort William to remain, as suggested by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon). I am sure all hon. members will agree that as applied to the average halfsection farm in western Canada to-day, it is below the cost of production.
I stated that I believed the floor price for wheat was of importance not only to western Canada but to agriculture throughout the dominion. During the last twenty-five years, in our agricultural economy in Canada, wheat has been king. If one were to follow wheat prices he would find that with very few exceptions-and these always where there were scarcities-the prices of other agricultural products have followed the trend in wheat prices. When we have had prosperity in western Canada and have had a good price for wheat, there have been good prices for other agricultural products throughout Canada. In those circumstances not only was there prosperity in agriculture, but that prosperity reflected itself throughout the economic life of the dominion. Prosperity in western Canada meant jobs in eastern Canada, better prices for fruit in British Columbia, and better prices generally throughout the dominion.
Wheat has been our greatest exportable commodity, and I believe it will maintain that position in peace time. The climatic conditions of a great area in Canada are such that not only is wheat the easiest crop to grow, but it is the most profitable. It will be seen therefore that a floor price for this commodity is of great importance to the country at large, and it has particular significance to-day because it gives some indication as to what the government's policy is going to be with respect to floor prices for other agricultural products.
Last year we passed floor prices legislation. The government stated that the legislation was being introduced for three purposes. First, it was to compensate agriculture for the low prices it had received for many of its products during the first two years of the war. During those years prices for agricultural products were really below the cost of production. I can remember in 1940 when there was a frozen wheat crop in northern Saskatchewan, the district from which I come, and our wheat was selling at from twenty-seven to thirty cents a bushel for feed wheat. We were buying British Columbia apples at S1.80 to $2.35 a box. It took five bushels of our wheat to buy one box of apples. That fall I had the privilege of visiting British Columbia, and I
saw some of the orchards in which these apples were being grown. I found that the fruit grower was getting from thirty to forty cents a box for his apples while he was paying $1.95 per hundredweight for our feed wheat. In other words it was taking six boxes of his apples to buy a hundredweight of our wheat, while it was taking five bushels of our wheat to buy one box of his apples. The result was that there were thousands of children in western Canada who never saw an apple, and many fruit growers in British Columbia were not able to diversify their production as much as they would have liked tio do. That, I say, was one of the reasons the government gave for introducing floor prices under agricultural products.
The other reason was to compensate for the price which agriculture might have received had there been no price ceiling structure in Canada. We all know that had there been no price ceiling structure, the prices of many agricultural products would have gone above the prices which were paid. The present legislation is being brought in recognition of the fact that the price of wheat probably would have gone to $2 or $2.25 per bushel if there had been no ceiling, and the same with beef and many other agricultural products.
The third reason they gave for bringing in floor prices was that it was to give the producer the cost of production. These floor prices were supposed to represent the cost of production of farm products, plus enough to give the farmer a return on his capital investment and a reasonable standard of living. I want to say that I do not think that the $1 per bushel for wheat will do any one of these things. That $1 per bushel for wheat is not $1 per bushel on the farm. It is really* 80 cents per bushel on the average farm in western Canada, and that does not compensate the farmer for the low prices he received in the early years of the war or for the prices he might have received had this order in council not been passed. Nor will it give him his cost of production plus a reasonable return on his capital.
If you are prepared to farm three, four or five sections of land as a corporation farm, it is jusv, possible that with economical management you might get away under the present legislation, but not under any other circumstances. I wonder if it is the policy of this government to have large corporation farming become prevalent in western Canada- because that will be the result of this present legislation.
This legislation is important because it indicates what the government's policy is
The Address-Mr. Wright

going to be with respect to floor prices under other agricultural products. It means a reduction from the present price of approximately thirty-five per cent. That is, floors under agricultural prices are to be placed at thirty-five per cent under the existing prices. I had a great many inquiries during the election campaign; and I have received many since, as to what I thought the government policy would be with respect to floor prices. I must say that at no time did I answer that I thought the policy would be a reduction of over fifteen, or at the most twenty per cent under present prices. But here we have legislation which is going to mean a possible reduction of thirty-five per cent in the purchasing power of the largest group in Canada.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I admit that if the legislation had not been passed we might have received higher prices. I believe the government at the present time is selling wheat in Canada for $1.25 per bushel for domestic consumption. That is being sold to our millers and the farmer is getting nothing.
