speechtext: Worse than that; the wheat board are selling it at seventy-eight cents to millers.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I was going on to say that not only were they doing that; they were paying a subsidy to the miller, which means that the miller was grinding wheat at seventy-eight cents per bushel, basis Fort William. I wonder if that is what the government considers as the floor price, seventy-eight cents per bushel, basis Fort William?
As I said, this matter of floor prices under agricultural products is one of the most important problems we are faced with in the (Mr. Wright.]
reconstruction period. It has to do with the purchasing power in the hands of a group of people which represents the greatest market in Canada. These people purchase more machinery, they build more houses, they buy more clothing and equipment than probably any other group in the dominion. If we are going to reduce their living standard by thirty-five per cent, I want to tell you that there will be a lot of people out of work in the next five years.
We are in favour of the quota system for marketing our wheat. I think this has been generally accepted in western Canada, especially the quota with respct to deliveries. It is good legislation and it has worked out quite satisfactorily. This $1 per bushel which we are getting under the proposal by the government as announced yesterday is not $1 per bushel for all the wheat we can grow in western Canada; it is only $1 per bushel for the wheat we grow under the quota, which is fourteen bushels to the acre on eighty per cent of our 1940 acreage.
What does that mean in income? I have a neighbour who is farming a quarter section. He has a family of six. Under the quota he can sell only from twenty-three acres, which means that he can sell fourteen bushels per acre from twenty-three acres of land. Anything he grows over that he cannot sell. I ask hon. members to use a little mental arithmetic to figure out how far that man can go toward clothing, feeding and educating his family on that sort of income. It just cannot be done.
I am positive that this floor is not the floor which will be accepted by the people in western Canada.
The minister has not given us any indication whether organized agriculture in western Canada was consulted or not, or whether organized agriculture in the whole of Canada was consulted. Was the Canadian Federation of Agriculture consulted? Were other farm organizations in Canada consulted? We do not even know whether the advisory committee to the wheat board were consulted.
The minister has not stated in this house, nor has any other member of the government, that this is a satisfactory floor so far as the farm organizations are concerned. I doubt very much whether it is. I know western Canadian agriculture well enough to know that it can never be a satisfactory floor for wheat from western Canada with prices where they are to-day for the things the farmer has to buy. We have no guarantee from the government that if wheat drops thirty-five per cent in price, the prices of the implements the farmer buys will go down with it.

The Address-Mr. Wright
Indeed, we know quite well from past experience that that will not take place. During the last war the price of agricultural implements and all the other items that enter into the farmer's cost of production went up and stayed up practically all through the depression. Prices increased then, and prices have increased since this war started, despite the price ceilings. Anyone who has bought agricultural implements knows that. I had to pay $2,050 just a few months ago for a tractor that I could have purchased for $1,600 in 1939, and that $2,050 was after removal of the ten per cent war exchange tax. The prices for the implements the farmer needs will stay up when our agricultural prices decline.
What agriculture in Canada wants is some tie-up between the floor prices the farmers are to receive for their products and the prices they will have to pay for the things which enter into their cost of production. That is what they ask for, but there is no indication of that in the legislation brought down by the government.
Here is another point. Is the. government treating all other industries in Canada on the same basis as agriculture? We have a government board dealing with textiles and a government board dealing with lumber. I have not heard of any price ceilings being placed on what the lumberman may charge for his exports. It is true that they can export only a certain quota, but for what they can export they can get any price that the buyer wishes to pay. Lumber is just as important as food to the people of Europe. I was over there last fall with other members of the house and saw the destruction of houses that had taken place in Europe. Houses are important just as food is important. Yet we have had no indication from the government that they intend to treat other industries in the manner in which they are treating agriculture. I hope the minister when he speaks will give us some such indication.
What does agriculture in Canada want?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: A fair deal.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Yes, my hon. friend says agriculture wants a square deal. That is all that agriculture asks for. Agriculture does not ask and has never asked for special privileges. Agriculture wants only a fair deal. It wants to obtain only its fair share of the national income, according to production and according to the number of people engaged in agriculture. That is all the farmers have ever asked for through their organizations, and they have never got it. The only time in my life when agriculture received its proportionate share of the national income was between 47696-22
1915 and 1919, during the last war. Even to-day, with agricultural prices where they are, agriculture in Canada is not receiving its proportionate share of the national income.
The farmers believe that they can do a lot for themselves through the organization of their own industry. They have asked this government to pass a natural products marketing act which would allow agriculture to organize so as to obtain the best possible prices for their products. They want a natural products marketing act which will allow organized agriculture, when a majority of the producers of any agricultural product signify their desire for it, to have a marketing board through which all of that product would be marketed, so that a small percentage of the growers may not be able to disorganize the whole market. They would be prepared to abide by regulations passed by the dominion government or provincial governments with respect to the quality of their products, so that the consumer would" be protected. Marketing boards and export boards which would take care of the exportable surpluses of agricultural products, so that when they were to be marketed in other countries the government would step into the picture and through longterm agreements with importing countries stabilize the export market-that is what agriculture is asking for.
Last fall I had the privilege of visiting England and talking to quite a few members of the present government there. I know that so far as the food of Britain is concerned, they do not want to see it go back into the speculative markets. They intend to buy through government agencies, and I am sure that they would prefer to deal with cooperative agencies and government agencies for their requirements in the countries from which they are importing. They would be prepared to make long-term contracts which could be negotiated on a satisfactory basis to both the consumers in Europe and the producers in this country. But the present legislation indicates just the opposite. It indicates that it is the intention of the government to go back to the marketing of wheat in the manner in which it was marketed in 1939, when the war started. That is, we are going to have a wheat board which will be prepared to accept delivery from the farmer. The Winnipeg grain exchange will function again, and growers who are not prepared to deliver to the board will be able to sell their product on the open market. The floor has been set so low now that it is going to force many farmers to sell on the open market if they can get an additional five cents a bushel for their wheat because the initial payment is not sufficient to meet their expenses.

The Address-Mr. Wright
But that is what your legislation amounts to, and that is not the desire of the western farmer as expressed through all his organizations.
The last resolution they passed asked for an initial payment of one dollar.
That was not a floor price. I know of no resolution that has been passed by any farm organization during the war which states that one dollar a bushel would be a satisfactory floor price for wheat.
They have passed resolutions to the effect that the initial payment should be one dollar. That is the last resolution they passed.
When was that passed?
That is an entirely different thing from a floor price.
It was the last resolution. It asked for $1 initial payment, and that is the only way under our system that a floor can be established, namely, by establishing the initial payment.

May I correct the hon. member's statement? The order, as I read it, does not set the advance at all. What the order says is that any time in the next five years it cannot be lower than $1; it can be set higher.

The Minister of Agriculture knows as well as I do that every time the government had done that very thing in the last years before the war, almost invariably the price of wheat went down and sat on that peg or very close to it during the full period. That has been the experience in the past and the minister knows that.
We are having a different story now.
That is what the story is, and I am telling the hon. member that he is telling a new story.

Maybe the minister does not agree with the policy of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) and is still fighting for a better floor price. I hope he is; I hope that the cabinet will listen to him. I know from experience in the past they have failed to listen to him in other matters.
The order in council the hon. member is discussing says that the floor shall not be less than $1. It does not say it has to be.
I am afraid the minister is making his old familiar play on words. He has done that and kidded the people of Saskatchewan for a long time, but he came mighty near to not kidding them the last time.
I was one of only four in Saskatchewan to have a clear majority.

That is simply because
there were only two candidates.
The other three are in the C.C.F.
No; two are over here.
Twenty-eight is a good majority!

I hope that, as indicated by the Minister of Agriculture, this is not the final word with respect to a floor price under wheat, and that we shall have a reasonable floor price set for that product. That is the whole basis of the plea I am making to the government to-day. I hope that they will bear it in mind and that it will have some effect on them.

Mr. Speaker, like the hon. member who has just taken his seat, I have been to a certain extent forced into this debate because of the announcement made, yesterday by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon). I am very glad to know that at least some of the ministers of the government are not satisfied with the meaning we took from that announcement yesterday. We are hoping that something better is coming about.
Before going on with what I have to say, I wish to thank the editor of the Ottawa Citizen, for the help he rendered in getting me back Htfr. Gardiner.]
to this parliament. The help was in the form of a left-handed compliment in an editorial of April 26 last. The editorial was obviously false and deliberately misleading. Of course the objective was the return of another candidate for the Battle River constituency. The editorial was widely advertised over the radio, in local weeklies, and in posters on many telephone poles in the Battle River constituency. However, the net result, thanks to the editor of the Ottawa Citizen, was that his candidate collected less than twenty per cent of the votes polled and made a contribution of $200 to the national treasury. I hope that the government will make good use of this money, because the man who lost it perhaps could ill afford to lose it.
On another occasion earlier in the session I introduced a bill to amend the Canadian Wheat Board Act. As I stated in introducing that bill the object was to do away forever with the Winnipeg grain exchange. On Monday last the hon. member for Winnipeg South (Mr. Mutch) speaking in the debate-and his remarks can be found at page 207 of Hansard- mentioned the fact that I had introduced, this bill, and undertook to uphold the grain exchange as an institution. I did not in any way attack the grain, exchange of any of its members, and I feel that the hon. member who took their part is perhaps one of the residents among the sleek and fat operators of that institution, while I am here interested in the lean, overworked and impoverished victims of that organization.
At page 207 of Hansard of September 17, the hon. member had this to say:
The Winnipeg grain exchange has been investigated by royal and other commissions more than a score of times within my own memory, and without exception it has been held to be making an important and worth-while contribution in the marketing of the products of the prairies. During the whole of that period it has been a simple matter in some sections, and in some areas it still is, to get an audience and a sympathetic hearing by detracting from that institution.
Any hon. member who is interested1 in the remainder of the hon. member's speech in that regard can find it at page 207 of Hansard as I
have indicated.
I think we all know, some of us from sad and costly experience, that the grain exchange is something like the gold standard. During the depression years of robbing the farmers and other classes in this country we stayed on the gold standard, but in 1940, owing to the pressure of war financing, we went off the gold standard. That, I think, is sufficient proof for us that, it. is not good in a time of

The Address-Mr. Fair
need. We also found that during the war practically all the grain exchanges in the British empire were closed down. The Canadian grain exchange was the last of them to close down, as far as my memory goes. I believe also we read in the press that Mr. Ranke, of the British cereals purchasing agency, refused to buy Canadian wheat if the exchange were left open. I remember also one of the senior members of the cabinet who has now gone to another section of parliament for security in his old days, possibly because: he was scared to face another election, went to England late in the fall of 1939.
As far as legitimate business of the exchange is concerned I believe that they are allowed to operate by legislation, but that legislation is not just as it should be. In the past we have had millions of bushels of wheat sold on the exchange that was never grown. It has been operated as a gambling den in most cases to the detriment of the farmers of western Canada. At the present time and for a number of years past the wheat board paid commissions to these operators, many of whom render no service whatever on sales of our wheat. I believe the same system is carried on in the old country where they are subsidizing some of the idle members of the exchange, so that they will have the gambling den all ready to set up after the war is over and the party is finished. I have often wondered why we did not sell automobiles and other types of merchandise on the exchange as wheat is sold. I am wondering why we do not put our money on the exchange or on some similar organization, and then we would hear some of those who are helping to conduct the Winnipeg grain exchange do a lot of howling. Personally, in case anybody should have any wrong impression as to where I stand, I am definitely opposed to the operation of the Winnipeg grain exchange for the sale of wheat or other grains. When I say that, I am uttering the opinion of all of the farm organizations in western Canada. The grain exchange is not run for our benefit. There is no question about that. I have taken part in the debate to-day and have said what I have because I believe the present policy of the government is heading us for further use of the grain exchange. If that is the government's programme, then I wish they had told the farmers of western Canada about it before June 11, and we might have had some different results on that day.
When the minister made the announcement yesterday I do not think he felt very happy about it. The minister is an honest man and knows conditions in western Canada much
better than some of the other members of the cabinet. I think he was a little bit ashamed when he made that announcement yesterday. Of course, it is in his department and there was nothing else for him to do but make it. I cannot agree with the interpretation the Minister of Agriculture places upon it.
In yesterday's Hansard we find the following at page 289:
In asking Canadian producers to forego such benefits as might be realized in the short run through higher export prices, the government recognizes the paramount need for relative stability of income to wheat producers. Toward this end, the government undertakes that in the five-year period ending July 31, 1950, producers will receive not less than $1 per bushel, basis No. 1 northern, in store Fort William/Port Arthur or Vancouver on the authorized deliveries for each crop year.
From the words "authorized deliveries" I take it that we are still to be on a quota basis. Let us go back a number of years and take the wheat crop of 1935. At that time, the price was established by the wheat board at 87i cents, as a concession, I believe, granted by a number of parties, the government, the wheat board, the grain trade and the pools. In any event, when I came to the house first the price was 87^ cents a bushel, but I think the house will remember that before long radical changes were made in connection with selling our wheat. We soon found the price down to eighty cents; then legislation was brought into this house fixing the price at sixty cents. Later someone wanted to get a pat on the back, and had the happy idea of raising it again to seventy cents. That figure did not mean seventy cents in the pocket of the farmer delivering his grain to the elevator. On the contrary, in my part of the countiy, for the average grade, it meant about forty-five cents for the best grain grown in the world. That price obtained until the 1941 crop was sold. For the 1942 crop the price went up to ninety cents, and in September, 1943, another change was made which brought it up to $1.25 a bushel. Now, in September, 1945, the Minister of Trade and Commerce tells us the party is over, that we are going to get down to business.
Perhaps some people think the farmers are getting too well off, and I readily admit that to-day they are in a much better financial position than they were when the war broke out. But I would point out also that farmers are working more than twice as many hours as any other occupational group in this country, and that their standard of living is not nearly as high &s that of most other groups. Now we are to get a floor price, but I am
The Address-Mr. Fair

afraid that after this year we are going to break our backs reaching down to that floor. That is what I was afraid of right along, when the legislation was brought in last year giving us guaranteed floor prices. No one even hinted where that floor price would be, and many of us were afraid it would be down in the cellar, that the legislation would be good for election purposes only.
I am not satisfied even with to-day's level of prices for farm products. It does not make any difference whatever what may be the prices for our farm products unless the prices of the commodities we have to buy are kept in line with them. During the years 1930 to 1940 the average portion of the national income received by the farmers of this country was 9-4 per cent. That is, 9-4 per cent of the national income went to approximately one-third of the Canadian population, who in most cases, as I have said already, were working twice as many hours as any other group. Even if we go back and take in a few of the good years prior to the beginning of the manmade depression, we find that the farmers of Canada, still representing one-third of the population, received only 11-3 per cent of the national income. If we take one specific year, 1932, we remember that many of us who had good crops at that time and hauled them to the elevators did not get back the cost of the threshing, and that year the farmers of Canada received five per cent of the national income. The Liberals were not in power at that time, so that we cannot blame them, although most people say the Liberals and Conservatives are alike. In any event nothing was done then to help the farmers. No move was made in the direction of cutting interest, the settlement of debts or anything of the kind to relieve the position of the farmers, with the result that we had to take it on the chin and come through as best we could. The condition that existed on the farms during that period is reflected in the statistics concerning the men who tried to enlist in the armed forces during the late war. In one case, out of 93,000 men who offered their services to the air force, only some 15,000 were able to pass the examinations, or one out of six, which is not a very good record.
I am not going to go into a great many details in connection with these matters, but I believe that the floor price should not be less than SI.25 a bushel for the next five years, with participation certificates issued for the balance. That will net us less than $1 a bushel for the average grade of wheat produced in my particular section of the country, and still will not give us our -proper share of the national income unless the prices of the 
commodities we have to buy are kept down or cut down and the prices of other agricultural products raised. This also would help to make up for the low prices we received during the depression and the early years of the war and would let us pay interest on the debt which, because of the policies of the different governments, accumulated during that depression period. At the present time labour is demanding a thirty-per cent increase in wages, and in some of the newspapers we read that labour wants a forty-hour week. Just where does the farmer appear in that picture? The farmer is not organized. Time and again I have told farmers that they have the remedy right in their own hands, and have tried to get them to apply it, but apparently some of them still have the wool pulled over their eyes.
We were not told by the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Finance that during the next five years prices of other commodities would be cut or controlled, and I am just wondering what their policy will be when they come to deal with some of the other commodities. As I said earlier, I believe the present programme is designed to prepare the lambs once more for the slaughter-house; that is, to prepare the farmers for the reopening and operation of the Winnipeg grain exchange. That is a definite detriment; and while twenty or more commissions have been appointed to look into the affairs of that institution, as was pointed out by the hon. member for Winnipeg South, my reply is that twenty or more white-washing jobs were done, through which the farmers can see very clearly. I remember that on one occasion we sent to the old country to get the services of an economist over there-Sir Josiah Stamp, I believe it was-and that he made an excellent job! But the fact remains that the grain exchange was in operation during the worst depression years we had, and that they did not in any way succeed in keeping the price of grain up where it properly belonged.
While I am speaking about agriculture, perhaps I might mention one other point, namely, the necessity for some amendments to the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. I suggest that act should be amended so that settlement might be made on an individual basis. In years past hon. members in this group have advocated that, time and again. I believe even the Minister of Agriculture would understand very well that a farmer on one side of a road allowance may have a good crop, because of rain, while the farmer on the other side of the road might not have had the rain and would therefore be without a crop. In my view this should be settled on an individual

The Address-Mr. Fair
basis, and we should also widen the scheme to include a proper and complete crop insurance coverage.
There is something further that is wrong in the act as it now stands. Some provision has, I believe, been made in the regulations. The point I have in mind, however, affects the farmer who is in a dry belt and qualifies for bonus, but moves out before a certain date in the fall. Even though he has incurred expenses during the year, he is denied the bonus provided by the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. This should not be allowed, and is a wrong which should be corrected.
Then, I say the eight-bushel yield is too low, and should be set back to the original twelve bushels an acre.
Then, in respect of a father and one or more sons operating their holdings with one outfit of machinery, I suggest all should be given the benefit of individual bonuses. Otherwise farmers' sons will be discouraged from starting up in agricultural pursuits.
I now come to rationing-and I have heard a good deal about it. I believe that the idea of sending meat overseas is a noble one, and that most people are in agreement with it. However, I have not yet heard of veiy many people who are in agreement with the programme or policy in that connection as set out by the wartime prices and trade board. I feel that this is one of the most disadvantageous times in which to bring it into operation, because we are now having large runs of cattle into the stockyards, and we find that the facilities there available are not adequate to take care of the offerings, unless, as the minister pointed out the other day, the stock can be shipped out at the rate of so many a day. I am not sure that that suggestion can be followed. It is something which may sound very nice, but the practising of which may present some difficulties, because of train services and for other reasons.
I do not believe that rationing will cure the problem. I think it will be found that large quantities of meat will spoil, as it did spoil on that earlier occasion when rationing was discontinued. Many people at that time refused to give up their meat coupons for cheap cuts of meat, or for the processed varieties. To-day merchants seem to be understaffed, and are complaining about the extra work placed upon them, _ if they are to keep records, and all that kind of thing.
Yesterday morning I received a letter which, in part, is as follows:
Why should meat retailers in the Dominion of Canada be on the dirty end of the stick because of the short-sighted policy of the Liberal government?
Any ten-year old kid could have foreseen a dropfin hog population with the existing differential between coarse grains and live hogs.
If Messrs Gardiner and Ilsley would use some of the money they have been taking from the public by taxation to pay a just price on hogs, we could have so many hogs that the existing facilities could not process them and meat rationing would not be necessary.
You can rest assured we do not intend to carry on under this system for many weeks. The amount of labour at our disposal will not permit us to comply with existing regulations, nor can we afford to pay for additional help solely to make up the innumerable returns and statistics demanded-
Unless meat rationing is lifted, without any doubt, a total strike of meat retailers across Canada will ensue.
Only this morning I sat in a barber shop for a few moments awaiting my turn. A man was in the chair and, although I do not know who he was, what he had to say about rationing, and what the barber afterwards told me concerning their general conversation, would not be allowed by you, sir, in this chamber.
As I said earlier, it is a noble thing to export our surpluses to feed hungry people in other countries. First of all, 'however, I suggest our own Canadian people should be fed. I believe, too, that other action might be taken which would help increase the production of stock, and possibly bring our production to a point where we could more readily feed other people, and ourselves as well.
In order to do this, I believe in inducements, rather than in compulsion. One inducement would be that the bonus of ten and fifteen cents a bushel on barley-I believe it is ten and twenty cents at the present time- which is being paid to hog or cattle raisers who do not grow their own feed, should be extended to all those who feed and market hogs, regardless of whether they produce their own grain. We may be told that this is impossible; but I should think our statisticians would certainly be able to estimate how many bushels of wheat, oats or barley, are required to raise a hog, under ordinary conditions. If a man receives pay on the basis of ten and twenty cents on the number of bushels used in raising a hog, I believe that the difficulty would be overcome. By that means I feel production would be encouraged, and I believe that some action along this line should be taken, because production in my part of the country at least, and I believe in other provinces as well, will decline much faster now that the war is over, and with conditions as they now obtain.
It has also been suggested that because we have very few veterinarians in the country
The Address-Mr. Fair

the government should assist in some way in training and in keeping these veterinSrians available. This is a profession which is not practised to any great extent to-day. Unless something is done the life of valuable stock will be jeopardized because of the absence of veterinarians in communities.
I have another item before mej one which I do not believe I could discuss fully before six o'clock. This would come under the heading of unfinished business; and when I say "unfinished business" I mean it was left over from the last parliament. I believe hon. members will agree it is one of those pieces of unfinished business which have followed the first world war and which have not yet been dealt with.
I have been glad to listen to so many young returned veterans from the war which has just been completed, and I hope that their courage in supporting the proposal which I make to-day, and which I have made on several other occasions, will not fail them, as it did not fail them when they faced the enemy. I would hope that before this session ends we would do something worth while for men who, in some cases, are the fathers of hon. members who represent constituencies in this parliament. I refer to the old soldier settlers from the first great war. As has happened after this war, a number of soldiers who took part in the first world war were recruited from farming communities. After the cessation of hostilities a number of these men decided they wanted to go back to settle on the land. After some sifting out, we find that 25,017 of these men were finally settled on the land under the soldier settlement board. The former Minister of Mines and Resources, who administered this scheme until recently, told us that the scheme was a hastily improvised one, and I agree with him. At the time these men were settled on the land there was advanced to them $109,034,331, which amounted to $4,358 each. The rate of interest was five per cent on current account and seven per cent on their accounts as soon as they went into arrears. They were given twenty-five years to pay.
I have a lot more detail which I am not going into. I wanted to give a rough picture of things, because anyone who is interested can find full details in last session's Hansard.
Hon. members will remember that agricultural, cattle and hog prices went down, and a number of these men found that they were up against an impossible proposition. First, the land was purchased at very high prices and even under ordinary conditions they would not have been able to make things go. When poorer times came there was nothing for them 
to do but to get out. Finally some sixty per cent of them did get out; they had sense enough to see that far ahead. However, many others who had not that foresight kept on battling against almost impossible odds.
I am using the date of March 31, 1944, as the cut-off date. If the government persists in its policy it will not be more than possibly ten years before most of these old veterans will be dead. The government will be able to get back the land and sell it possibly to some Japs or Germans or Italians at one-half of the cost of the land as they are doing under present circumstances.
The total amount repaid was $75,888,550, made up of $50,507,493 principal and $25,381,060 interest. I am giving these amounts separately because I should like hon. members to note that during the same period the cost of administration of the soldiers' branch only was $27,340,763 or approximately $1,100,000 a year for the period under review. If you take the interest of $25,000,000 and the cost of administration of $27,000,000 you have a total of $52,000,000 odd. The amount of principal repaid was $50,507,493. A number of necessary adjustments were made amounting in all to $44,000,000 up to the end of March, 1944, at which time there was a total amount outstanding of $7,715,954.
At that time there were 6.153 men still remaining on the fend. By that same date only 4,130, or sixteen per. cent of the original settlers had been able to obtain title. The 6,153 who were still on the land represented twenty-five per cent of the original number. The average indebtedness at the end of March, 1944 was $1,254. I am bringing, in this amount for a definite purpose. The original debt of these men was $4,358 and, after twenty-five years' hard work, in many cases persecution by the officials of the board, each man srtill owed an average of $1,254. That is equal to twenty-nine per cent, of the original purchase price. Under the present Veterans Land Act a veteran who keeps up his payments over a ten-year period gets a grant of $2,320 which is thirty-nine per cent of the original amount of credit extended to him. On many occasions the government has made promises to these men, and that is exactly what another government did. I have here an address of Sir Robert Borden, then Prime Minister of Canada, which he made in 1917 to the Canadian expeditionary forces. He said:
The government anti the country will consider it their first duty to see that a proper appreciation of your effort and of your courage is brought to the notice of the people at home, and it will always be our endeavour to so guide

The Address-Mr. Fair
the attitude of public opinion, that the country will support the government to prove to the returned man its just and due appreciation of the inestimable value of the services rendered to the country and empire; and that no man, whether he goes back or whether he remains in Flanders, will have just cause to reproach the government for having broken with the men who won and the men who died.
Similar promises have been made by the present government and I hope they will make a better job of living up to them. Back in March, 1941 an order in council was passed which I think is of interest to all Canadians. It has made many of us hang our heads in shame. At that time it' was found that a number of veterans of great war I were enlists ing to serve in the second great war. A number of these old veterans were soldier settlers and they found they could not keep up their payments. They saw a way, at least for the duration of the war, to provide a means of livelihood for their families and they enlisted. No payments were coming into the soldiers settlement board, and on March 19, the treasury board, on the recommendation of the former Minister of Mines and Resources passed this order in council;
The board has had under consideration a submission of the honourable the Minister of Mines and Resources reporting that:
1.	A considerable number of persons who agreed to purchase farms from the soldier settlement board or from the director of soldier settlement on long term contracts have enlisted in the Canadian armed forces.
2.	In many cases the dependents of such enlisted persons continue to occupy their farms but no provision has been made for payment of instalments in respect of their contracts or of taxes in respect of their farms.
3.	The director of soldier settlement has no authority to carry such accounts indefinitely and it is considered desirable to provide for deduction from dependents' allowances to cover local taxes and interest due.
Accordingly the board recommended . . .
That is the treasury board about which we have heard so much, the board that has so much control over parliament and to which some consideration should be given at an early date.
. . . that notwithstanding any provision to the contrary contained in any of the regulations providing for payment of dependents' or marriage allowances in respect of dependents of members of the Canadian armed forces, that in all cases where the dependents of an enlisted person continue to occupy the farm for which such person is indebted to the director of soldier settlement and in respect of which the contract terms are not otherwise satisfactorily provided for, there may be deducted from the dependents' or marriage allowance amounts sufficient to provide for payment of taxes levied by the local taxing authority in respect of the property
in question and interest accruing annually on indebtedness to the director of soldier settlement, such deductions to be made monthly and in no ease to exceed $20 per month except with the consent of the dependents concerned.
Promises were made to these men after the first great war and definite promises were made during this war; yet we find that order in council in operation. In the case of the ordinary man who enlisted in this war for the first time there are no deductions from the allowances paid to his wife and family. But those fellows who have offered everything for the second time are penalized simply because they have entered into a contract with the soldier settlement board and are not able, on account of conditions man-made, artificial and deliberately planned, to make their payments.
Again, for those fellows who felt they had a little longer lease on life than some others and wanted to continue, order in council P.C. 10472 was passed on November 19, 1942, providing that those settlers with courage who wanted to try to carry on a little longer could bring their cases before the board or committee that was set up, and if that committee saw fit it could reduce the man's indebtedness by a certain amount, and give him a further extension of twenty years in which to pay off his indebtedness-forty-five years of his life to pay for a quarter-section of land and starve himself and his family in the process, simply because of the policies designed by this and former governments.
The action of the government in bringing down the price of our wheat to $1 a bushel for the coming five years is a challenge to the men who are settling on the land under the Veterans' Land Act at the present time. By that act-and I expect that policy will be continued-the government are making it impossible for any man, no matter how hard he works, or what kind of farm he may buy, to carry on and ever get possession of his home. It does not take many years, even for those who have established themselves in the farming industry, to find themselves thrown out on the road, as many of my neighbours have been in past years, when they are compelled to sell below cost of production and pay exorbitant prices for everything they buy. Before this order in council is made effective the government should review its whole agricultural policy and programme and take into partnership with them representatives of the farm organizations and have the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) divorce himself from his unhealthy and unholy matrimony with the banks and other financial institutions.

My first desire in rising to speak this evening is to put the house at ease, and I do not think I could do better than to announce that my remarks will be brief. I wish, however, to preface them by extending hearty congratulations to you, Mr. Speaker, on the great honour that has been unanimously conferred upon you by this house. In the last parliament you, sir, and my very humble self had a close association in being seat-mates in what you might call the suburbs of the House of Commons. Now we are separated by distance. There is an old adage that says, "absence makes the heart grow fonder." If I might be allowed to change the wording I would say that distance makes the heart grow fonder, and that would be applicable to our associations at this session.
I know, sir, you are quite conscious of the fact that with the great honour bestowed upon you there goes a great responsibility, and knowing you as I do, I realize your willingness to assume that responsibility. I know also you are quite competent to discharge the duties which will devolve upon you, and I think I can speak on behalf of the house when I say that in the performance of those duties you will have the cooperation of every hon. member. The very unanimity displayed in appointing you to the position you hold is a prelude to that cooperative assistance which you will receive.
I wish also to congratulate the mover and the seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne, and right here I think I should compliment those who had the selection of those speakers. I think their choice was splendid inasmuch as they selected two hon. members who had contributed a great deal to the conflict of war. Now they come into the house and are just as solicitous and as ardent in the conflict of peace. Young men as they are, they have projected, in this conflict of peace we are now undertaking, thoughts which may very well be given consideration in the rehabilitation and reconstruction era.
I have listened to the speeches delivered in this house and I have nothing but congratulations to offer; but if I may be allowed to be critical on one point it is this. I do not like that mist of gloom they seem to cast over the country now that we are undertaking a conflict which is just as serious as the conflict of war. Comparing the visibility of affairs in Canada to-day with conditions six years ago, one can say that six years ago the 
people of the Dominion of Canada were suffering the agonies of the damned and at that time they had very little hope of redemption. Finally peace came. The war was won and it was won at an exorbitant price. It was won in suffering; it was won in losses irreparable; it was won in the agony of our loved ones and in the torture of the innocent. That was the price we paid for war. A new era has now arrived. We are given an opportunity now to show whether we are worthy of that redemption, and I think the outlook is not too gloomy.
We have to-day in Canada, fortunately, a government that has carried on a gigantic war effort. We have a government that not only prosecuted the war successfully but have brought down measures designed to deal with the problems which they anticipated would arise and which are arising at the present time. When this conflict of war was on we in Canada were fortunate. We were fortunate because we had at the head of our war departments men who not only had great experience in military affairs but had the wisdom to select an executive that was competent to initiate, develop and carry on to a successful termination a gigantic war effort. I say we are fortunate in that we must always remember that despite the efficiency of our war ministers very little could have been accomplished in this war conflict had it not been for the cooperation we received from every element of our Canadian citizenship. Our labour men, our industries, our farmers, our fishermen, our transportation facilities and everything that could be integrated into the war effort assisted. Our young men volunteered and went willingly to the front; and comparatively old men, men who had passed middle age, who in the last war had gone through the experiences, the sacrifices, the hardships and the miseries of that struggle, volunteered and stood in arms to protect our country. Young women who were occupying lucrative clerical positions left those offices and went into war industrial departments and undertook the onerous employment of making implements of destruction.
Our people were not only generous; they were tolerant. They were generous to a degree. They gave not only of their savings but of their earnings to war bonds to supply a fund for Canada to carry on our gigantic war undertaking. They accepted the restrictions of rationing and all other regimentations without a murmur. They complained very little about the ever-increasing tax imposts. They regarded these as a matter of war necessity.
As a matter of fact, our civilian population conceived the idea that this was an all-out

The Address-Mr. McGarry
war effort, and while they could not display the same equality of sacrifice they at least offered equality of service. There was something else that they did. They maintained the morale of the nation. Valour is a virtue. There is no doubt about that. It was a necessary virtue of those who were standing in arms against the aggressor. But it is no more a virtue with the fighting forces than it is with the civilian population, whose thoughts are bound up with those brave men who have to undergo the dangers of every day and face the uncertainties of the morrow.
So I say that while incidentally it may appear that I am offering some eulogy to the government, which they well deserve, neither this government, however efficient the ministers in the war departments might be, nor any other government, could have done what Canada did had it not been for the cooperation of our Canadian citizens. Let us not forget that the intelligentsia of Canada are just as much concerned in this conflict of peace to-day as they were in the conflict of war. Therefore it does not behoove us in the House of Commons to be throwing misty or gloomy shadows in front of the effort that is now being presented to the people of Canada. Six years ago I was not so hopeful that the conflict of war would be won. To-day, because of the measures that this government brought down in war time to deal with such great problems as unemployment, 1 am hopeful that we shall win the conflict of peace. I am perfectly sure that the speech from the throne reflects the spirit of a policy which will bring about a happy and successful rehabilitation and reconstruction programme.
When a country is at war there are two responsibilities which devolve upon the government. The first is to supply men, money and materials to carry on war projects. But just as important is the responsibility of maintaining the economy of the nation. I believe that this government did a very good job in that field. Mark you, three hours after war was declared this government established the wartime prices and trade board. We all know the effect of that action. The effect was that there was a check-up on hoarding and profit eering. We all saw the result of that. We did not see, as we did in the last war, men waxing rich on the blood and sacrifice of the people; we did not see our prices mounting to a dizzy height as they did in the last war, and when the fall came, not to ordinary peace-time level, but below, it was responsible for the depression which followed. The action taken by the government is one of the things which has kept Canada economically sound, and has
made for a proper distribution of wealth throughout the nation.
May I recite just a few of the measures that are not promises but measures which are operative at the present time. First of all, there is the Unemploment Insurance Act. That is certainly going to serve a great purpose now It was timely inasmuch as it was introduced and put into operation at a time when there was no unemployment. The result is that today we have a repository of cash which will certainly render auxiliary assistance in the days of transition when there must necessarily be some unemployment. Mention might also be made of the amendment to the Land Settlement Act, a great improvement on the old act. It not only improved it but extended it. Then there was the compulsory employment act.. One could recite many measures. These were all brought into force and will be of auxiliary service in this transition period. When we add to that the proposed measures contained in the speech from the throne I, for one, am greatly surprised that some hon. members say that this government has no plans for the future. I cannot see where there has been one omission. There was no lack of provision for what might be anticipated by any sensible government. I cannot understand why hon. members say that there is no planning. It must be that they have not followed the history of this government since 1940, or they say it for some ulterior purpose.
Inquiries have been made in the house as to whether or not the war was terminated so far as Canada is concerned. I do not think we can give an intelligent answer to that question until we find out the meaning of the two words -war" and "peace". I shall quote what one authority says about the definition of war. This is Webster's definition of war. He describes war as being "the absence or cessation of peace or cooperation; that condition of a nation or a community which is not at peace." Therefore, if we were to judge from the remarks of some hon. gentlemen opposite, we would come to the conclusion, following that definition, that Canada is still at war.
And will be for some time.

To confirm my theory of war, let us look at the definition of peace. Peace is "active cooperation by means of spiritual, mental and material forces between nations, states and rulers, and between parties in the same nation and state; the employment of spiritual, mental and material forces against evil powers at home and abroad, such as ignorance, injustice, ugliness, disease and intolerance." When these agencies are eliminated we are supposed to be at peace; but whatever
The Address-Mr. MeGarry

the meaning of the words may be, we cannot have any peace in Canada unless we have the active cooperation of these mental, spiritual and material forces.
Canada did not enter this war as an aggressor; she entered it for the purpose of preserving our democratic rights and to establish a lasting peace. Paradoxical as it may seem, it was necessary to go to war to have peace; we won military victories, and finally we won the last and most essential victory. But in a war for peace military victories are only milestones which mark the pathway that will lead to the haven of peace. But there is another conflict in which we must take part; we must enter into it with the same generosity, the same spirit of cooperation and tolerance as we did in the conflict of war, because I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, it is just as serious a conflict.
I would say to my hon. friends opposite, be a little patient; remember that we are only just now at the transition period between war and peace. 1 do not think any hon. gentle man can suggest more than this government is going to do, some of winch it has in operation and some to be put into operation before this session closes. No one can deny that we have wise and effective planning, and I would say to these hon. gentlemen that they should not expect performance before planning. Take a little time. It took the greatest Creator and Builder of all six days to make this world. Now we are trying to build a better world, and some hon. gentlemen think that should be done, with our efficient ministers, in two weeks. They should not speak in that way: they should not be spreading these words of gloom among the people. If that sort of thing had been done at the beginning of the war, possibly we would not have come out of that conflict as successfully as we did. I am absolutely in earnest about that. Let no one make these gloomy assertions that we are working in the dark. Visibility is good, but, as I said before, we must cooperate; we must have generosity; we must have tolerance, and we need every help the people of Canada can give.
To the government I would say, make as much haste as you can. Translate into performance the plans already laid down; and when this programme of reconstruction and rehabilitation is under way, do not forget that you cannot have absolute peace in Canada while there is one section discriminated against, one section which does not fit into the general picture. I have certain appeals to make to the government in regard to my own constituency. I am not going to present them 
now, but I say that if we want to have peace and contentment in the whole of Canada we must see to it that no section of this great nation is listed among the forgotten units.

Mr. Speaker, it appears that new members are having a field day, so to speak; and, being a new member, I wish to take this opportunity of discussing some serious problems pertaining to the constituency of Medicine Hat, which I have the honour to represent. As many hon. members know, my constituency was represented in the last parliament by Doctor F. W. Gershaw.

A
good man.

A very good man and a very good friend of mine, and a gentleman held in high esteem by all who know him, regardless of their political views. I am pleased that he is now in the upper house, and I am sure southern Alberta will be well represented in that chamber by Senator Gershaw.
I regret that I am unable to use the expression of some hon. members in describing their constituencies. I have heard many of them say theirs were the best constituencies in Canada. I can say that the ueople of Medicine Hat constituency are the best people in Canada; and if I cannot say that Medicine Hat is one of the best constituencies, that is because of the inaction of the federal government. When I say that I include also our Conservative friends to my right, because, after all, they were in power for a few years and nothing much was done in my constituency. We did sell our wheat for twenty cents a bushel, and our hogs for two to two and a half cents a pound, and I do not forget that in 1937, when the present government were in power, they purchased a good deal of stock in that area at the handsome price of one cent a pound, so that they did not do so very much better. From this I believe hon. members will understand what I mean when I refer to the inaction of the government.
The largest part of my constituency is in what is known as the drought area. We have an average rainfall of from seven to nine inches. A few small portions may have an average of twelve inches, but that would be only a very small part. We have three irrigation districts. The first is the eastern irrigation district at Brooks, comprising some 1.500,000 acres, with approximately 200,000 acres irrigable. This project is well known for its high production not only of grains but of alfalfa and all kinds of field crops, and also

The Address-Mr. Wylie
the large number of dairy herds of good quality stock. They also take great pride in the wonderful buildings in that area, the homes of which they are so proud. This project is also known all over western Canada and parts of the United States for the wonderful pheasant shooting which may be enjoyed there. Thousands of dollars come into that area every fall from this source alone, and every available room in the town of Brooks and throughout the district is reserved a year ahead.
Then we have the Canada land and irrigation project at Vauxhall, which is much the same as the Brooks project, though not quite so extensive. Finally we have the Taber and Lethbridge irrigation district, which is known for the production of sugar beets. Here we have an industry that fits perfectly into the general irrigation farms programme. The growing of sugar beets gives the farmers a hoed crop which keeps their land clean, gives them an assured price for their product, and yields valuable by-products utilized in the now extensive live stock industry, which takes in the winter feeding and finishing of 25,000 head of cattle and 100,000 head of lambs. The Lethbridge feeder association alone does over a million dollars' worth of business each year. The sugar beet industry brings into the country several million dollars' worth of new wealth a year. The area under sugar beet production is approximately 30,000 acres; many growers are harvesting from twelve to fifteen tons or better per acre and receiving around S10 a ton for their deliveries. In addition, they have the valuable beet tops, beet pulp and molasses from the Raymond and the Picture Butte factories, at a nominal figure, for live stock feeding. Production has reached a point where additional factory space will be necessary, if production is to be stepped up; and the Brooks project has gone on record as wanting a factory. I see no reason why they should not have a factory. I know that all arrangements were made about two years ago for a sugar beet factory. The only thing required to establish it was a permit from the dominion government; but this permit, as the residents of the Brooks area know, was rejected.
Since coming to this part of Canada I have heard it said by many people that sugar manufactured from sugar beets is not of the same quality as that manufactured from sugar cane, and that fruits preserved with beet sugar will not keep. A statement of that kind is, in my opinion, entirely wrong. I believe that we in Alberta will recognize good, canned fruit as quickly as would any others, and I am quite sure that any canning done with beet sugar
will keep just as long as if it had been done with sugar cane.
When I go back to Alberta, or perhaps before that time, I am going to suggest that the best thing our sugar factories can do is to put on an advertising campaign so as to advertise their product properly, and to let the people in eastern Canada know that we have just as good sugar in Alberta, produced right in that province, as is found anywhere else in Canada. It is an industry for which there is a big future, a future in which not only Alberta but all Canada will share. There is no reason at all why we should not be producing four or five times the amount of sugar we are producing to-day. I am sure most members from Alberta, and especially those from the southern part of the province, will recognize the truth of that statement. Southern Alberta's sunshine and fertile soil combine to produce flavourful vegetables, with the result that we have the development of the vegetable factories processing some 7,000 acres of peas, corn, beans and turnips. In addition, the only dehydration plant in the province is situated at Lethbridge for the processing of carrots, table beets, potatoes and turnips. In addition to all that, dairy herds have been improved and cheese factories are set up throughout the district.
From what I have said respecting his constituency it would almost seem that I am boosting the constituency of the hon. member for Lethbridge ('Mr. Blackmore). However, it shows what can be done by means of irrigation. In the greater part of my constituency we have two proposed irrigation schemes, namely the St. Mary-Milk river and the Redcliff-Ronalane. I am sure many hon. members have heard discussions in the house respecting this problem, and will remember particularly the contribution made to that discussion by Senator Gershaw. I do not think a session went by without the senator's having discussed that matter. Might I reiterate that, usually, before election there was a little more stress put on it. However, that is something which is essential to the welfare of that part of the province.
During the last election campaign the Liberal candidate for the constituency of Medicine Hat said that unless the people voted Liberal they wmuld not get irrigation. Then, on the night he was defeated he said that he was pleased to see a Liberal government returned to power, but that the people of the constituency of Medicine Hat would still have to get in touch with him before they could get any government jobs.
The Address-Mr. Wylie

What about the
hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. MacKinnon) ?

And the hon. member for
Edmonton West too; there should be plenty of support from the hon. member for Edmonton West. The government should move now to give official approval to the building of the transcanada highway and the completion of these irrigation projects by voting in the new estimates a sum large enough to permit a start on these projects.
We should have more industries in the west. When I refer to the west I am thinking, of course, of Medicine Hat in particular. We have an abundance of natural gas. Few people realize the benefits to be derived from natural gas. As Rudyard Kipling once said, Medicine Hat is the only city in Canada with all hell for a foundation. All we have to do is to drill a hole, put in a pipe and there you have power, you have heat and you have light if you wish. I should like some of the eastern members to come out to that area and see what can be done, not only in the city but in some of our ranchers' homes. We can certainly do with more industry in the west.
I have listened with a great deal of interest to what has been said about the housing problem by members on both sides of the house, especially returned men. Hon. members on this side of the house who have returned from the war are just as anxious to have a housing programme that will work as are hon. members on the other side,. They want the same thing. What they want are houses. They want a programme with action, not just talk.
I know as far as my own city is concerned, there has not been a single house1 built there by wartime housing or with government assistance. It was suggested that we could put in a small holding project of one acre plots outside the city limits. The land was surveyed several times, but it was decided it was not suitable because it would cost too much to put water on it. The majority of the residents never did think very much of that project and the city council and citizens of Medicine Hat could see no reason why returned soldiers should be placed outside the city limits. We believe that they should have the privilege of living with the other residents right in the middle of the city. There are lots available there for their homes, and the city council is quite willing to give them lots of from
fifty or seventy-five feet by one hundred and thirty feet if the government will apply this project to the city. I believe that this proposal should have consideration by the government, and that Medicine Hat should have the benefit of small holdings within the city limits. We have plenty of lots right on the power line where all services would be available. After all, we all want the same thing; we want homes; but the whole building project is not advancing very fast. It will require the cooperation of everyone and of all governments to get the project really going.
I was pleased to see that the government is proposing to make changes in the Old Age Pensions Act, although I am disappointed that these changes may not apply until 1948. It is very nice to know that when you reach the age of seventy the means test will be done away with. However, I agree with the leader of this group, the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low), that the age should be reduced to sixty years and the pension increased to $50 a month. I am sure that there is not a member of this house who would wish to live on a pension of $30 a month at the age of seventy or even sixty.
In the very near future I am sure that all civil servants, provincial and dominion, as well as the employees of most concerns, the Canadian Pacific Railway Company included, will be pensioned off at the age of sixty. The C.P.R. have that now, I believe, in some of their departments. In the civil service in Alberta the pension age is sixty-five; I am not sure about other governments, but I am quite sure that it will not be very long before they will all be superannuating at the age of sixty. I believe that is a good plan because it will enable people to enjoy a little pleasure in their old age, especially if the pensionable age is reduced and the pension increased to at least $50 a month.
I should like to say a word about education. I believe that the time has come when we should have uniform standards of education from one end of Canada to the other and that the government should make grants to assist in higher educational standards being attained. Education is the main training for any young person; it is something that will stay with him or her through life, and the more education they can have the better. I agree with the hon. gentleman who has just sat down (Mr. McGarry), that Canada has a wonderful record so far as the war effort is concerned; I also agree with what he said as to the sacrifices that were made by our boys, and I believe that if we will only work as hard to win the peace as we did to win the war we
The Address-Mr. Bryce

shall have homes for these heroes and a decent Canada for all to live in.

Mr. Speaker, I am in the fortunate position that I do not need to come to the house to tell about my constituency of Selkirk, because anybody who has gone to school has read about those hardy pioneers from my native land, the Selkirk settlers, who came up the mighty Nelson and up lake Winnipeg and settled at Selkirk, Fort Garry and along the Red river valley. Later on, people came there from Iceland, people with a democratic point of view which has enriched our own democracy. Still later, we had people come to us from the Ukraine and other parts of Europe, who have helped to develop that great interlake country and have added to the wealth of Canada.
When I sat in the last parliament, Mr. Speaker, I was many times reminded that there were only two official languages in the House of Commons. I can assure you, sir, that my French has improved slightly but my English is no better. I should like to remind you, sir, of that age-old alliance between Scotland and France and to assure you that your countrymen and mine still respect that, and I am quite sure that when you think about it you will have no difficulty in understanding what I want to convey to my hon. friends on the other side.
The hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) asked the other day when the war would be over, and there was quite a little amusement among hon. members when he asked that question, but I can assure them that it is a serious question for the dairy farmers to-day. The dairy farmers are being kept in business by a subsidy. The consumer is able to buy the milk his children require because of that subsidy, and I should like the government to come out and tell us if and when it intends to cut off that subsidy. The dairy farmer wants to know that so that he can plan his work. How long will this subsidy last? I do not know whether the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) or the government can tell us that, but it is something that the dairy farmers require to know, and know pretty soon. We have practically no butter in the country. The government at the present time is paying ten cents a pound subsidy to make it possible for our farmers to produce cream. It is a disgraceful state of affairs that the dairy industry has to be subsidized by ten cents a pound to produce butter. Where will our butter stocks be if that ten cent subsidy is taken away? We shall be in a deplorable state. The dairy business is not

something that you can go into to-day and step out of to-morrow. You have to plan ahead and make arrangements; you have to get the feed up this summer that you will use next spring. I appeal to the government, through the Minister of Agriculture, to let us know something about that in the near future. It would be nice to know, too, when the subsidy to the millers is coming off wheat.
I should like to add a few words to what the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Wylie) said a few minutes ago. He talked about the beet growers. I am interested in beet growers, because we took a great deal of trouble in Manitoba to set up a beet factory so that we could establish a better way of farming and get away from straight grain growing. We set up that beet factory for that purpose, but the position to-day is such that we can hardly keep going.
I do not want to go over the whole thing again. The hon. member for Medicine Hat explained how we can feed pulp in the winter time and make as good sugar from beets as ever was made from cane. They were good enough to invite me to their meetings, and since they are constituents of mine I feel it my duty to bring their demands before the house.
