The Winnipeg grain exchange is pretty close to me and I endorse everything which the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Fair) said. I say to the government or any other government that follows it, heaven forbid that you should ever reopen the grain exchange, because every particle of stone, brick or lime in it was paid for by the sweat and toil of the western farmer. Do not ever forget that. Do not let it come back again. The wheat board has done a good job. It is not often that I hand bouquets to the government, but I say, you did a good job this time, although it can be improved on. In a world such as Henry Wallace talked about when he wrote of the century of the common man, did he expect that in 1945 or 1946 we would go back to gambling in the produce of the farmer? Certainly not. You can never again justifiably have gambling carried on with the produce of the farm. I am saying in pretty blunt words what I mean, but I mean it from the bottom of my heart when I say that we should never again allow gambling in this way. I do not think any man should have the right to gamble in the food of a nation; it should never be tolerated. I have nothing against the men on the grain exchange. They are all good fellows. It is the principle of the thing that I am thinking of. Why should they be parasites on the other fellow? Maybe I have said enough about that because I know there are a lot of people who want the grain exchange back. I do not know what the government was thinking about. I say to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) that he controlled wheat, barley
and oats, and then he took over the flax and did a good job on the whole lot. Then he left the smallest crop so that they would have the thin edge of the wedge to start gambling again.
What about September rye? When the farmer sold his rye on September 21 of last year, he got ninety-one cents. Look at the newspaper to-day and see what the price is. It is 81.621.
The same old story.
That is the same old story. They did it with the wheat and they are still doing it with the rye. I say, shame on the government for allowing them to do it.
Coming through the rye.
I am sorry that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) is not in his place at the moment, because if my constituents ever get him back in Selkirk-
He will never be in his place.

-they will have a lot to say to him. In the first place the income tax level is too low. An exemption of $660 and $1,200 is not good enough.
May I come back to the dairy farmer? Nobody in this country has exploited his family like the dairy farmer, and I am one of them. When my children were going to school they had to milk the cows before they went, so that we could send milk to Winnipeg to have some money to spend. These things are not taken into consideration by the income tax people. It is unfair. What about the farm woman? The Minister of Finance said last year that every woman would want the same concession if it were given to the farm wife. I say that the farm woman does far more than the city woman. She has to get up in the early morning to have the breakfast ready for the men to be in the field at half-past six. Then she has to wash dishes the last thing at night. No city woman does that. The sooner the Minister of Finance revises the income tax regulations, the sooner it will be safe for him to go back to Selkirk.
I do not wish to say very much more about cream production, but the income tax is a big handicap to getting cream to-day. In the constituency of Selkirk there was one man who had not filled out an income tax form. The forms were brought in and he was asked about it. The reply was that he had never earned enough money to fill in one. The inspector said to him, "You received so much for your grain?" The man said, "Yes." The inspector
The Address-Mr. Bryce

then said, "You sold some cows; what else did you sell?" He said, "I sold an old steer." The income tax man added these things up and made up a statement. He then said, "You sold some cream." The reply was, "Yes, we took a few cans of cream." The income tax man said, "Well, the dairy company in Winnipeg said you sold $400 worth of cream." He then tallied up the income tax form, gave him credit for the number he had in his family, and said, "You will have to pay income tax on $400." The farmer then got into the old car, or maybe the old buggy, and drove home. He then began to think about it. You see there are some people like that; they take a little while to think. He thought about it and he found that he was paying income tax on $400 that he and his family had earned before breakfast and after supper, and he said to himself, "I will never milk cows for Ilsley." The upshot of it is these cattle go to market and the country is deprived of another supply of cream. I want the government to take that into consideration. The man who is working a double day producing that cream before breakfast and after supper is entitled to some consideration in the income tax regulations; and do not let us forget the woman on the farm, because we would never get along without her.
Last year I asked the Minister of Agriculture some questions about condemnation insurance, and he assured me he would look into it.
I am looking forward to having him tell us something about it because it still is as bad as it was. I showed the house that in 1943 the packing industry of Canada got about $800,000 more than they were entitled to in condemnation insurance alone. The figures all appear in government publications; there are no figures of mine in there. It is a disgrace that that should go on. They have given us a new schedule in the west, and they take so much a head, fifty cents for a female animal and thirty cents for a steer, half of one per cent on hogs, and so on. Why should that thing go on when we have established tuberculosis free areas in Manitoba? I live in a T.B. free area. Why should I have to pay condemnation insurance to the packer when I have no T.B. animals? Condemnation insurance has become a racket and the government should look into it. I can see the minister smiling.
I assure him this is a serious business. We are still working on the T.B. insurance that was established a number of years ago when cattle were worth fifty or sixty dollars apiece. When I replace an animal in my herd to-day I pay $150, but I get only $38 from the government when they come and take it away because it is infected. That should be revised. 
I ask the. minister to revise that. Something should be done about it, because it is not a square deal.
I want to be as brief as possible, but I should like to touch on the cattle situation to-day. A few days ago the minister made a statement in which he said that we can be sure of the price for twelve or twenty-four months ahead. That is not the case. If I sell steers on Monday and get twelve cents for them and send the same quality of steers on Thursday and if there are plenty of steers on the market the packer will pay eleven cents. The only thing that happens is that the farmer loses another twelve dollars and the packer makes it, because the animal goes into the same grade as the ones he bought on Monday. The reason the twelve cents were paid on Monday is that there was not enough cattle on the market to bring down the price; on Thursday the market is perhaps flooded. Perhaps I can explain better what I mean if I quote from the Ottawa Journal of Thursday, September 13: Board buying surplus lamb
The meat board is buying surplus Canadian lamb for export to Britain.
For lamb of exportable quality, and of 38 to 55 pounds cold weight, the board is paying one-quarter of a cent per pound below the ceiling in each marketing zone.
These lamb purchases, together with the board's action in buying all surplus mutton since July 24, assure Canadian farmers and ranchers a market for all their surplus lambs and sheep, said J. G. Taggart, chairman of the board.
That is not true. If there is a lean, market it will work. The only person this protects is the packer. There is neither ceiling nor floor on live animals; it is only on the dead animal; when these lambs are dead they will be protected and the packer will have a market for them. But let you or me strike a market such as we had a year ago, when there were nine thousand lambs and sheep at Winnipeg; the minister knows what happened. We pleaded with him to open the market to the south; that was done, and what happened next morning? The packers had said they did not want those lambs; they were too leggy; they were thin; they were a poor type. Everything was wrong with them, but when we received the telegram from the minister saying that the market was open, the next morning the Winnipeg market rose $1.50, and one of the packers who said he did not need any lambs bought sixteen double-deck carloads. That is what happens, and I am sorry the government makes regulations like that. There is no protection for the farmer in a flooded market, because the packer can go in

The Address-Mr. Black (Cumberland)
and buy at h'is own price. I used to blame the Minister of Agriculture for these things.
I used to think the packing industry dominated the Department of Agriculture. Now I am satisfied that the packers dominate the government. That is the state of affairs which exists not only on the Winnipeg market but on other markets. The farmer has no protection whatever when he goes to the market; he has to take what he is offered, and the packer, being, a shrewd business man, will buy at the lowest possible price.
We also have that situation in the fish industry. Look at the fellow who catches the pickerel in lake Winnipeg; he gets ten cents a pound; but when I go to buy that pickerel in the store in Winnipeg I pay forty-seven cents a pound for it, filleted. There may be some fish men here, and I want them to understand that I know a little about fishing. I have been there in the winter and taken the fish out of the nets, and I have been there in the summer time also. When a fish is filleted it may lose fifty per cent. That would make it equivalent to twenty cents a pound, but there is an awful killing for someone between twenty cents and forty-seven cents. The primary producer, the man who risks his life to get the fish, does not receive his fair share. I asked about that. I went to the fish packers and asked why there should be such a spread between the amount paid the primary producer and the retail market price. They replied, "Oh, we have nothing at all to do with that. Donald Gordon set the price." Well, Donald Gordon needs to revise his prices.
Recently in this house, Mr. Speaker, we have heard quite a bit about rationing. I do not object to rationing; I am all for it if it is going to spread the meat farther. I think the mistake made by the government was in removing rationing when they should have kept it on. I imagine they would begin to see their mistake last February or March, and they should have started rationing again at that time, but I suppose it was too near the election for them to risk it. Let us be fair about this. I have my own flesh and blood in the old country, and to-day they are eating less than they did during the war years. Those are the people who came through the blitz. We know what our own boys have done and what they have suffered. Do not let us kick about a little rationing in order to let the other fellow have something that is coming to him. Some time age I read a stoiy about a prominent citizen of Ottawa who was visiting the ruins in England during the blitz, when people were being dug out and so on. A little
fellow came along and for something to say the gentleman from Ottawa asked, "What do you hope to be when you grow up?" The little lad replied, "Alive." Let us be true Canadians about this. Any sacrifice we make will be nothing compared with what they did for us.
I want to get finished within my time, Mr. Speaker, or I shall not be able to say I was brief. After reviewing all these things I believe it is apparent that the putting into force of the necessary long-time agricultural policy, which should be in operation, is prevented through the domination of government policy by the meat packers, the millers, the sugar combines and so on. The result is that the primary producer is left with uncertain returns and at the mercy of big business.

You have been offered many congratulations, sir, but the best I can wish for you is that at the end of your term you will prove to have been as acceptable to this parliament as your predecessor was to the last parliament.

These men and others we of this parlia-liament miss. But we are glad to welcome the new members. Especially I would welcome the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Merritt), a man of whom everyone in Canada and in the allied armies is proud. I am also pleased to have in his proper seat our leader, Mr. Bracken. Throughout all his life he has served the public, and I believe he has still a greater service to render to his country. It is a great misfortune that party leaders have such difficulty in gaining election to parliament. Surely that is a reflection upon the voters and the opposing parties. One can look over the history of leaders of political parties in Canada, and he would recognize at once how unfortunate it has been that they have had so much difficulty in having themselves elected-and I am sure the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) will agree with me in this.
There are many subjects with which I could deal, but I shall make my remarks fairly brief. The subject of greatest concern in my province, is the future industrial prospects of Nova Scotia and, in particular, the county of Cumberland. It is only fair to say that they are very much disturbed, very much worried.
To-night I am going to read some of the statements made on Monday of this week by the Minister of Reconstruction (Mr. Howe).
I have done what I could to assist him during the war, when he served as Minister of Munitions and Supply. At least I have not made his work any more difficult, and I have endeavoured to uphold him both in the house and in the country. I assure him I will give him all the support of which I am capable in the great task that is his in this period of reconstruction.
The people of Cumberland and of Nova Scotia generally have been very much disturbed, but if they could accept the statements made by the minister they would be completely reassured, and would feel that they could take their place in the industrial life of this country.

In the statement of the Minister of Reconstruction to which I listened on September 17, and which I afterwards read, he said, as reported at page 223 of Hansard:
I see nothing disturbing in the present situation as far as employment is concerned.
My constituents, and the people of Nova Scotia generally, will be very glad indeed to receive that statement, if they can believe it and if that promise will be fulfilled. In my town of Amherst there was an industry employing 3,000 during the war. The staff has been reduced to about 300, most of whom are working on inventories and records.
At a later point in his speech the minister said:
One thing that is abundantly clear is that there are at this moment two jobs open for each and every applicant for a job.
That is welcome news for people in my constituency, if they accept it, or hold the minister to his assurance.
Again he said, on the same page of Hansard:
The work of reconstruction has been in progress since early in 1944 and has been accelerated since the establishment of the Department of Reconstruction in the summer of 1944. The work divides itself into the following branches:	First, over-all planning
including studies of economics and statistics; second, industrial reconversion; third, research and development; and, fourth, control and distribution of materials.
My people in Nova Scotia will want to know what planning there has been; they do not know. They will want to know what industrial reconversion there has been in their province; they do not know. They want to know what research and development there has been; they do not know. They want to know what control and what distribution of materials there has been.
I could make many other quotations from the minister's speech, but I must hurry on. He stated further, as reported at page 225: Reconversion is also under way in war plants owned by the dominion government. This is more difficult in that a sale of the plant to private industry usually is involved. For some months we have had a fairly definite idea of the nature of the peace-time industry which would use each government-owned plant.
We have government constructed and owned plants and buildings in the town of Amherst, and our citizens are most anxious to know what has been done or is to be done with them.
Further on he said:
As nearly as possible we endeavour to keep each plant in a line of work comparable with its former employment in order that the workers living in the vicinity may find employment in the same plant without too great a change of skills.

The Address-Mr. Black (Cumberland)
That is the best news the town, of Amherst and people in other parts of Nova Scotia have heard since V-E day or VM day, when our forces became victorious. But they want a little more evidence that this policy will be applied.
Then he goes on to say:
A limited number of war plants are being retained by the crown and rented for multiple occupancy as an incubator for small industries. Here again the demand for space exceeds any reasonable supply. The most promising small industries are being given preference, and it is expected that from these multiple occupancy plants will develop industries which will in time build and occupy their own premises.
That will be great news for the people back home. Then the minister goes on:
It is quite obvious that during 1946 we may expect an expansion of peace-time industry comparable with the expansion of industry generally during the war years. Many of the largest expansions of industry yet to be reported are now being processed in the Department of Reconstruction.
We would like to have more detailed information with respect to that policy as it applies to our part of Canada. Then the minister goes on:
In our earlier studies of requirements to provide continued full employment we estimated that one million jobs in excess of those obtainable in 1939 would be required. I can report that the one million additional peace-time jobs are definitely in sight, and that there is little likelihood of any over-all lack of employment in the near future.
The province of Nova Scotia and the other maritime provinces consider that it is within their rights to share in this reconversion and industrial expansion which the minister promises will be forthcoming to Canada. Many of our work men and women are walking the streets and many have had to leave recently for central Canada in order to obtain employment. I could go on to give further quotations and hold the minister to an accounting and ask that he apply these assurances to our part of Canada. I believe the maritime provinces have earned a right to sympathetic and fair treatment. I will help the minister; I will help the government and I believe every member of parliament should do everything possible in order that the maritime provinces may participate and share in this industrial activity or expansion that he promises is coming to Canada.
I do not want to make any complaint, but -our part of Canada was the last to get wartime industry. The work men and work women of Amherst were enticed away, as were the people in the rest of the maritime provinces. I have under my hand advertisements which appeared prior to the establishment of war industries in our town by which working people were induced to go to central Canada. Here is one which reads:
Wanted
Women to work in a war industry.
Fifty miles outside of Montreal.
Must be between the ages of eighteen and forty.
Here is another one:
Wanted
Girls to help in the production of munitions which are urgently required by our armed forces, the war industry near Montreal requires immediately girls for the following classes of work:
A-Cartridge machine operators.
B-Cartridge inspectors.
C-Matrons.
D-Stenographers.
E-Typists.
F-General office clerks.
While we were slow in getting under way, we have made a good record. I believe the Robb engineering works has made as good a record in the production of shells as any plant in Canada. But this industry has now had to let out a large number of its experienced and skilled help. We have a good clothing industry and we have an aeroplane industry that employed, as I said, three thousand men at one time, but which now has only three hundred. Six or seven industries in the country were given the responsibility after the battle of Britain of assembling and building the Avro-Anson training plane, and one was located at Amherst. The first Avro-Anson training plane that flew in Canada was built in the Amherst plant. Many of the workmen in that plant were not trained, but they were natural mechanics. They felt they had a high duty and responsibility, and the result was that they did such efficient work that they built the first plane put out by any shop in Canada.
Certain information was brought out in the war expenditures committee, but we are not supposed to refer to it and I do not intend to do so. However, information came to me from other sources that the Amherst shop gave the best results of any aeroplane factory in Canada. It was not perfect because there was some waste and lost time; nevertheless its record was the best. They got the best results. The Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) will confirm that because he got full cooperation from labour, which gave him no difficulty whatever. I have here a report by the minister of labour of Nova Scotia which was given publicity on September 6. It reads:
Another high achievement has been emblazoned on the war record of Nova Scotia, it was ascertained yesterday when Hon. L. D.

All I ask on behalf of the people of Nova Scotia, of the maritime provinces generally and of my own constituency is that they be given an opportunity. It is the duty and responsibility of the minister to see that this is done. Our part of Canada has played its full part in building up Canada. It has played its full part in the war. Enlistments there have been as high as in any part of Canada. It has played its full part in industry. All it asks now is that it be given an opportunity to have a place in the peace-time industrial life of Canada.
The working people of Amherst will cooperate with the minister. I believe that every member of this house should be anxious to see Amherst and other places in the maritime provinces have a share in the industrial activity under reconversion. I do not want to take up much time but there are a few matters I should like to deal with.
During this session reference has been made to the building of the St. Lawrence waterway. I think the people of Canada are satisfied that that great waterway should be built. I am in favour of it, but I make this condition- and I believe every member from the maritime provinces should support me-that at the same time the Chignecto canal should be built. This portage was used by the early French settlers three hundred years or more ago when they crossed the isthmus of Chignecto. The building of this canal is justified from a commercial point of view. It is justified also from a defence point of view and we should have the cooperation of the United States in its construction. It would have justified itself in the last great war, and we in the maritime provinces are entitled to have this construction proceeded with. Cheap power should be available, either by the construction of power plants on the Petitcodiac river or by the use of coal at the mine mouths. With this power available, industry in the maritime provinces would be on a parity with industries located along the St. Lawrence waterway. I appeal to the

people from all over Canada to see that some measure of fairness is extended to the people of my part of Canada.
I want to refer to the ferry boat Kipawo, which with its predecessor plied, between Wolfville and Parrsboro' across Minas basin for forty years. It is the only ferry service in all Canada that has been discontinued during the war. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) will bear me out when I say that it was discontinued' because the boat was needed for war purposes. I ask that that boat and service be restored.
I also ask that greater measure of justice be extended to the people of the maritime provinces as regards the cost of many commodities which they buy in central Canada. I .pointed out to the house in the previous parliament that bicycles, for instance, with a ceiling price were sold at higher prices in the maritimes than in any part of Ontario or Quebec. Automobiles and trucks are also sold at higher prices in the maritime provinces than in central Canada. If we cannot build these articles and many scores of others in the maritime provinces I believe that there should be an equalization of freight rates so that the people of the maritime provinces will not be penalized by having to pay higher prices than are paid in central Canada.
In Nova Scotia there is also the question of the sugar refinery which was closed down in the early days of the war. I saw a short time ago a ship of 6,000 tons discharging its cargo of raw sugar at Halifax harbour, and that sugar and following cargoes were shipped through Nova Scotia to be refined elsewhere, while our Nova Scotia industry was idle.
The rolling mills at Trenton have been closed, and now the users of secondary products have to buy many of them in central Canada and have delays and the additional freight rate to pay in getting them delivered to their machine shops in the maritime; provinces.
I want once again to refer to the marsh lands, and in this I know I have the support of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner). The marsh lands are deteriorating year by year. They are the most fertile lands in all Canada. While millions are being expended to develop virgin areas in the west-and I have supported it-we have never been able to have ainy complete programme undertaken by this government to protect these marsh lands from the tides, to drain them, to utilize their fertility. We had the assurance from my leader when he- was in the maritime provinces that such a programme- would receive his

Mr. Speaker, some members are crying "question," but I have not taken up very much of the time of this house, and I am pleading now for some measure of justice and some measure of appreciation with respect to what is required in the maritime provinces.
A great duty devolves not only upon this government but upon the Canadian Car and Foundry company, which had its inception in the town of Amherst, its first president being the Hon. N. Curry. But central Canada has drawn its activities away from Amherst. Canadian Car and Foundry has a great record in this war. Its production has totalled over 1300,000,000, and it has paid out in wages $121,000,000. It has undertaken projects for the British government, the United States government and the Canadian government when other industries were loath to do so. I repeat, it has a great record in the war, but if it is to be a real Canadian industry carrying the confidence of all the people of Canada it should make it its duty to see that some post-war industry is established in the town of Amherst that will employ one thousand workers. I appeal to the government to see that that company gets all the assistance to which it is entitled and that every means is taken to bring about the establishment of such an industry in Amherst.
I am not going to take up any more time, but I have felt it my duty to place before the house the situation as regards the maritime provinces, Nova Scotia and my own constituency of Cumberland. The Minister of Reconstruction and Supply gave a glowing report to the house the other night, but I want to tell him that the people in my part of the country are much disturbed over what is to be their fate in the post-war years, and they will hold the minister and the government and all the members of the federal parliament to an accounting that in the years that are ahead a greater measure of justice be done to the people of the maritime provinces than has been done in the last twenty-five years.

I wish to embark upon a subject which has not been mentioned this session and which indeed, during the time I have been in this house, has not been given the attention which I believe it deserves. I refer to the question of electoral and parliamentary reform. I do not speak on this subject with a claim to any superabundance of knowledge by reason of any particular research I have conducted. I base my arguments purely upon my own observations after sitting in this house for several years.
I have concluded, Mr. Speaker, that the most futile business in the world is that of a private member of this house. I have a desire to bring about in Canada a parliamentary system which at all times will get for the people the results they want. I notice quite a number of new faces in the house, quite a number of new members, some of whom I believe are distinguished gentlemen. I understand there are some who have the distinction of having won the Victoria Cross. I believe we have in our midst some high ranking military men. We have one hon. gentleman, who was also here in the last parliament, who on one occasion was lieutenant-governor of Ontario. These men should be of inestimable value to this country; but as time goes by and they sit here I think they will discover that their business here as private members is just about as futile as anything in the world. We have in this parliament some young men with all the exuberance and ambition of youth; someone has said that this is a young man's age, and I am glad to welcome these young men into parliament. I do not agree, however, that this is particularly a young man's age; I rather agree with Henry Ford, who a few years ago said that if you took out of the world all the brains over sixty-five you

The Address-Mr. Hansell
would not have enough brains left to run it. I suppose these young men came into parliament with visions of doing great things. As they sit here as private members, I am afraid it will not be long before they will be sadly disillusioned. Before I came here to the session a gentleman stopped me on the street and said, "I believe parliament has been reduced to nothing more than a glorified debating society".
You said it.

It was said by a gentleman in my own town, whose name my hon. friend would1 not know. He was a good Conservative, but that does not make any difference. I replied, "Well, you are wrong. It is not even a glorified debating society". It is not even a good debating society, for in a debating society the side that has all the arguments can win on points, but that never happens here. It does not make any difference who has the best of the argument; the government always wins. Before we ever start out in a debate we know who is going to win. So I say it does not make any difference how logical an argument may be, or how forceful it may be; the government always wins.
When parliament opens it does so with a good deal of pomp and dignity. There is the firing of guns, the playing of bands and the officials dressed in their official robes. Soldiers are there as their bodyguard; the mounted police stand at attention dressed in their bright red tunics, and the whole thing gives a tremendous air of importance. I have no criticism to make of that. Perhaps it is as it should be. But sometimes I wonder if all this is simply to fool us into believing that we are really going to do something.
I am sure we are glad to welcome the leader of the official opposition (Mr. Bracken) to the House of Commons. He is a public servant paid for guiding the opposition in the house. I believe he should be paid. Further, he should be paid all he is getting-and he should try to get all he can. I am inclined to believe that the leaders of other parties should also get just a little more for their efforts. However, be that as it may, what happens? In reality, what is happening is simply this, that the leader of the opposition is paid to be an expert in argumentation- and nothing else. Because even he, no matter how forceful his argument and no matter how logical, can never expect to win. The government always wins. And whether it be he or the leader of any other party, no matter how they may feel about their work, they are private members just the same and, so far as power is concerned, they have no more 47696-23
power in parliament than the little page boy who sits in a dignified position at your feet, Mr. Speaker.
The government is all-powerful in these things. What I am calling for is a real, democratic parliament. I am calling for a type of electoral and parliamentary reform under which each and every member of parliament would be directly responsible to the people of his constituency-and nobody else. But what we have in our present parliamentary system is not that. Let no one think I am wholly against the party system; what T am against is rigid party machinery, whereby a man when he is out stumping for the election is bidding for the people to send him to parliament on the basis that he will do what they want, but when he comes to Ottawa finds that he has to do what his party leaders want. That is the thing I criticize.
For what reason does this parliament exist? What, in reality, is its purpose? I do not know that I have ever read a definition of it, but I have prepared one of my own, and I would like hon. members to tell me if there is anything wrong with it: The Canadian parliament exists for the purpose of passing such legislation as will give to the people of Canada the results they want. I do not think there is anything wrong with that as a definition of what this parliament should be. But may I ask this:	Do the people of
Canada get the results they want?
No.

Of course they do not.
Did they get the results they wanted between 1930 and 1940? Are the old age pensioners to-day getting all the results they want? We could go through the whole gamut of public life in Canada, and I am quite certain we could not say that the people have had the results they wanted.
Why not? Well, if parliament is here to legislate, surely it should be able to legislate without fear or favour, and with no strings attached, party or otherwise, so that legislation would be put on the statute books of Canada which would give to the people exactly the results they want. To a great extent, they do not get those results because of the impotency of parliament. Believe me, it is a brave man who will rise in his place on the government side of the house and vote against his party because he stands for great principles.
I am convinced that under our present electoral and parliamentary set-up the only democracy we have in Canada is the right to cast a ballot-and democracy ceases at the ballot box. Just the same, may I say I was very

appreciate that applause1 or not. What I am against is government policy. I believe their policy is all wrong. I have offered these suggestions which I think are reasonable ones. What I say is all in favour of the argument for some type of electoral and parliamentary reform. I believe that there should be some reform of the senate, but I am not going into that to-night except to say that seats in the senate should be won by election and not be granted by appointment. But seats in the senate have largely become a system of political rewards, and: that should never be in a democratic country.
A word about money. Why should the government say: We cannot do anything because we haven't the money. Let parliament tell them what should be done. We do not say: You cannot run any trains because we have no tickets. We do not say: You cannot make any cloth because we have no more yardsticks. We do not say: You cannot have any roads because we do not have any miles. Physically it is possible to do all these things. If this parliament should decide that a thing is physically possible and desirable, that should be legislated, and the government of the country, who are supposed to be the ser-
